The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects in exploring dark matter
particles weighing less than GeV/c$^2$. Its ability to detect dark matter is
powered by a $^136$Xe rich detector located at the LNGS laboratory under
extensive rock coverage, spanning 360 km$^2$. 

By utilizing R&D we have developed a radical new approach to dark matter
research in calorimeters, combining ultra-pure amorphous CmTe crystals with a
temperature measurement system employing a sensitive superconducting SSI-SQUID.
 

We have successfully tested the first prototype of our specific design,
featuring an amorphous CmTe crystal with a 0.3 mm thickness and a 0.05 mm^2
surface area, connected to an SQUID through an ultra-pure and thin heat-sensing
channel. 

We have conducted a series of measurements during low background levels and
found that the temperature resolution reaches 2 eV over a 0.2 Hz frequency.
Additionally, our results demonstrate the ability to discriminate even the most
aggressive dark matter models, differentiated solely by their crystal structure.

We are now preparing to integrate these new detectors into the CRESST experiment
in time to contribute to the upcoming dark matter research in the next science
cycle.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, resolved by restricting either the image or a blur kernel representing blur. Differing from prior research, this study regulates the structure of the blur kernel. The kernel mixture concept utilizes Gaussian kernels with enhanced scale and center configurations, producing a nearly non-parametric blur shape representation. The decision of the base kernel count becomes more flexible due to a data-driven method. This strategy is successfully tested in a satellite imaging scenario where it outperforms current standards regulating latent images in favour of the kernel's structural adjustment.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant BiHom-bialgebra with quasitriangular properties and show that the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation of weight -1 can be derived from a unitary quasitriangular covariant BiHom-bialgebra. Lastly, we outline two methods for constructing BiHom-pre-Lie modules from Rota-Baxter paired modules.

Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for thoroughly
examining software adherence to specifications through precondition/postcondition
declarations. The improvement of semantic parsing methods and increasing
computational capabilities enable the extraction of formal logical structures (terms)
from spoken or written language with growing precision and scope.
  Although various research projects focus on using Hoare logic for security,
  a prominent formal method like Hoare logic remains unsuitable for natural
  language, leading to the necessity of new approaches. In contrast to prior
  solutions, this work uses Hoare logic as a foundational framework and
  demonstrates a semantic method for generating, with and reasons, Hoare-like
  preconditions and postconditions using natural language statements.
  The method involves (1) translating Hoare-like preconditions into
  conditionals with the help of a parser, (2) generating Hoare-like
  postconditions by identifying an end state described in the original text,
  and (3) extracting certain action effects from the text to form postconditions.
  The method was tested on a tree-bank of 2K Hoare-like preconditions and 4K
  action effects with various degrees of accuracy (99\% and 94\%, respectively).

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within each tree level. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when handling failures that don't directly affect performance, leading to the development of RCanopus. RCanopus enhances Canopus to not only tolerate various types of failures but also to guarantee the accurate detection and recovery of failures and protect against malicious attacks, all while maintaining compatibility with the original Canopus code base.

Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, which examine linear transport properties, have yielded contrasting results when analyzing the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing solely equilibrium experiments, not linear transport properties, indicating that one may be necessary but not sufficient for understanding the effects of cholesterol. Our findings derived from free energy differences and equilibrium experiments reveal that the generalized Gibbs-Douglas moduli relate to long-range curvilinear stresses, which are maintained in equilibrium through mechanisms like longitudinal stress adjustment and fluid flow. We propose that the gel-liquid transition in cholesterol's influence on membrane curvature involves two distinct regimes, during which the cholesterol molecule interacts with areas exhibiting curvature-induced non-uniformity in molecular distribution. We model these processes using a power-law for cholesterol's membrane binding, which is consistent with Michaelis-Menten kinetics and facilitates investigations into equilibrium stresses, fluctuations, and phenomena like membrane- protein interactions and membrane instability associated with cholesterol. Our analysis may be expanded to other membrane components like lipids exhibiting non-uniformity in molecular distribution.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its modified Friedmann equation is analogous to that of the APS LQC model. Notably, the model's critical matter density at the bounce point is a quarter of the original APS LQC model's, with the critical density $\rho_{cL}$ equalling $\frac{\rho_c}{4}$. This discovery implies that quantum gravity effects will manifest earlier than previously thought and also make detection potentially easier due to a lower critical density.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made available 
for close examination, in addition to seven events used to establish the energy 
scale for the Auger topology-based energy scale. A separate table lists all 
detector stations involved in each event, along with their associated readings.

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions. Researchers have developed uncertainty estimation methods for deep object detectors but found them unsuitable for robots due to their non-deterministic outputs causing false positive detections. To resolve this issue, we propose novel metrics for evaluating object detection uncertainties that take into account a method's predictive distribution and are applicable to both deterministic and stochastic models. These metrics are then used to assess the performance of cutting-edge object detection uncertainties methods on two popular datasets, showcasing their effectiveness in creating more reliable detectors for robotic use.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems.
Current traffic prediction methods, largely based on deep learning techniques such as CNN and RNN, accurately predict traffic but are vulnerable to overfitting when dealing with changes to test data distribution, leading to a decrease in prediction accuracy over time.
In our research, we investigated how breaking down test data into smaller, locally-focused sections, known as patches, can mitigate these distribution changes and improve the precision of traffic predictions.
By using a dynamic prediction framework that combines the strengths of both patch-based and segment-based approaches, we demonstrate that patch-based learning can help the prediction model adapt to changing traffic patterns more effectively.
Using real-world traffic data from cities like New York and Seattle, we compared the effectiveness of our proposed approach against traditional traffic prediction methods and found that patch-based learning outperforms these models and achieves superior accuracy.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been used to create systematic approaches to proving coherence in strict higher categories. We're taking this theory further by applying it to Gray categories, which can be thought of as a specific type of tricategory. To achieve this, we need to adapt rewriting theory to the context of precategories, which encompasses Gray categories, and allows for automated calculations. Our findings demonstrate that precategories with a finite rewriting system have a limited number of critical interactions that can be quickly calculated. We also broadened the scope of Squier's theorem to fit our research framework, which led us to the discovery that convergent rewriting systems lead to coherence in Gray categories, implying that equivalent parallel transformations are inherently equal. We've further utilized this result to prove coherence in monoids within a Gray category and extended this principle to complete and complete semicategories, which led us to the creation of Squier's theorem for Gray categories and tricategories as a natural consequence.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We have developed and validated an open-source, state-of-the-art deep learning method that uses an extended 2D multi-orientation approach with automatic pre-processing and orientation alignment. We compared this method to three recent networks that use an atlas-based approach in two epilepsy datasets, finding it outperformed them in accuracy. Additionally, we found our approach successfully adapted to new epilepsy datasets without re-training, demonstrating its ability to generalize across different clinical populations and configurations.

We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with only one path occupied at a time. We investigate various possible explanations for the emergent effective single-particle system and find that these accounts are unfounded. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the desired outcome is achievable through classical simulation. Ultimately, we conclude that the reported data does not provide conclusive evidence for the occurrence of the quantum pigeonhole effect.

Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor responsible for the formation of high-energy inner proton radiation belts. A Monte Carlo simulation model is created to calculate proton radiation at low Earth orbit by simulating the interaction between cosmic ray particles and the Earth's atmosphere, followed by transportation in the magnetosphere. This includes modeling proton generation from neutron decay and trapping within the geomagnetic field. To tackle the associated computational difficulties, we develop an optimized algorithm that reduces computation time, using three-dimensional Earth models for atmospheric and magnetic-field conditions. Our findings show good agreement with Ap8 proton data from the Interstellar Boundary Explorer mission. Satisfying accuracy is achieved with fewer grid points than traditional methods, significantly reducing computation time to less than one-hundredth of traditional approaches. This improved model enables the simulation of protons at various geomagnetic conditions, allowing for the generation of controllable reference databases for various low Earth orbit missions.

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This 
paper proposes a novel three-phase training approach based on expressivity 
criteria, consisting of global model reduction, weight refinement, and weight 
redistribution among links. To address information transfer bottlenecks, we 
propose a pyramidal framework, subsequently examining and addressing network 
topology clustering for link reconnection purposes. Our experiments, 
involving node classification tasks, demonstrate a substantial improvement in 
terms of speed and robustness, providing insights into neural architecture search, 
specifically the importance of link reconnection strategies.

To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a novel
noise-based method ensuring differential privacy. This method incorporates
noise with characteristics inspired by the Huber loss function in robust
statistics, and is termed as the Huber mechanism. In our study, we evaluate the
performance of this Huber mechanism against other privacy mechanisms, including
using the Alternating Least Squares solver. A range of experiments are carried
out on artificial and real-world datasets to assess various aspects of the
Huber mechanism. These experiments aim to examine its influence on prediction
accuracy, row completion percentage, and computational time. At the same time,
we verify the effectiveness of ALS as a solver for low-rank matrix completion,
as well as examine how different parameter settings impact matrix reconstruction.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust', and tiny particles, known as PAHs, come in various distinct forms. The evidence suggests that a uniform grain composition is most consistent with the observed patterns of infrared polarization, and the established ratio between optical and infrared polarization. A detailed analysis reveals that a combination of astrodust and PAHs accurately replicates the properties of galactic extinction and emission from interstellar dust while adhering to existing constraints on dust abundance. The associated data and software have been made publicly accessible for further research.

Research on exoplanets has led to groundbreaking discoveries surrounding low-mass stars, like those at TRAPPIST-1 and Proxima Centauri, but theoretical models fail to account for the formation of giant planets in such environments. Recent high-resolution ALMA observations of CIDA 1, a Taurus low-mass star, show disk substructures indicative of a massive planet. Our aim is to simulate CIDA 1's dust ring using a model that combines a low-mass planetary skidmark with a low-mass disk. Planets as small as 0.3 times Jupiter's mass could form around low-mass stars, given suitable disk configurations. Following a planetary instability, a low-mass planet like CIDA 1's perturber could result in a massive dust ring, observable at sub-millimeter wavelengths. Our simulations indicate a 30% chance of detecting the perturber via direct imaging and suggest a more extensive sample of similar systems is needed to be obtained through sub-millimeter observations of optical spectrosopic surveys.

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with vertices of clickable lights. Each click affects the state of the chosen light and its neighboring lights. A sequence of strategic clicks leads to winning, which means turning off all lights in a predetermined arrangement. Inspired by the original Lights Out game from Tiger Electronics, we're investigating an extension known as the Most Clicks Problem, which revolves around determining the most clicks required to solve any given arrangement of lights on a simple graph. By establishing a set of criteria we call $S_s$, this study provides a framework for identifying the least clickable arrangements of lights and offers specific conditions for determining when an otherwise unclickable arrangement can be solved. Additionally, our analysis yields a solution to the Most Clicks Problem for certain types of graphs, specifically those with a certain number of edges and an arrangement of lights that are all on an unclickable combination.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and multi-channel image datasets. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art segmentation models in terms of segmentation performance, especially for images contaminated with noise or blurriness. To assess the segmentation results, both boundary precision and region classification accuracy were considered.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily switching from an initial approximation to a more precise one, trying to minimize the accuracy loss later. Theoretical justification for this approach is given, along with a demonstration of its applicability to various established analysis techniques.

A broad range of structural phases in perovskite oxides host various physical properties, one of which is topological phonons. Topological phonons are characterized by their unique phonon topological structure, exemplified by key materials like bismuth and silicene. Through density functional calculations, researchers have detailed the phonon topological properties of (BNH$_4$)O$_2$, finding that it exhibits topological phonons in multiple phases. Notably, BNH$_4$O$_2$, a compound in the Pmmn structure with a significant intramolecular interaction, displays a significant reaction to external pressures, transitioning into the Im-2m structure. Further calculations reveal that BNH$_4$O$_2$ exhibits both topological phonons and near-free molecules simultaneously, contributing to its dynamic properties. Long-range external influences do not disrupt the topological phonons within BNH$_4$O$_2$, but significantly affect its near-free molecule phase, indicating a versatile response to external pressures. Investigating BNH$_4$O$_2$ may provide valuable insights into a new class of near-free molecule materials.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their adaptability in generic metric spaces. Large-scale data processing in these fields requires more efficient algorithms to handle distance-based outlier detection effectively, given the growing availability of powerful computational environments. Building a main-memory index has proven to be an effective solution, offering fast detection possibilities. Our proposed method capitalizes on a novel proximity graph, offering substantial performance improvements over the current state-of-the-art solutions.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is built on two core components - the first enables the construction of equitable neighborhoods for any node in a graph and the second allows adaptation to specific tasks. Inspired by constraint generation for fairness, we introduce the notion of 'neighborhood descriptor'. This descriptor captures key characteristics of a node's surrounding environment and can be used to represent different types of neighborhoods. Through extensive testing on six graphs and six GNN models, we observed substantial improvements in fairness for both static and link prediction tasks, resulting in a significant reduction of adverse bias by 30.88% on average. Our work sets the stage for a comprehensive understanding of neighborhood fairness, sparking a new wave of research in this underexplored area of fairness for graph-based machine learning.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a comparable level of accuracy.  Supporting Matlab codes for both methods are provided in the appendices.

Theoretical physicists conduct experiments in final stages with data obtained from proton-proton collisions, utilizing the CMS detector at CERN's HL-LHC, a more powerful version of the Large Hadron Collider. A specific study focuses on high-energy collisions producing squarks and second-generation supersymmetric particles. Researchers used simulated data based on random models to create histograms of energy patterns left behind in the CMS detector when squarks and gluinos are produced. These simulations cover a wide range of theoretical possibilities regarding supersymmetric particle properties. When the decay process involves virtual squarks, the study can rule out a gluino with mass under 2.1 TeV when it decays into a squark and missing energy particles. Gluino properties that decay into three quarks or a quark and virtual squark are also explored, yielding a 95% confidence upper limit of 1.23 TeV on the gluinoid mass-velocity relationship when the decay product travels a long distance from the collision point. A specific model involving light supersymmetric top squarks is used to create detailed simulations of energy patterns in the CMS detector and compare them with actual data from 2016 proton-proton collisions at high energies. These simulations cover a wide range of supersymmetric particle properties, demonstrating a high probability of producing supersymmetric top squarks in proton-proton collisions. A statistical analysis of energy patterns in the CMS detector shows that a two-body decay process involving the supersymmetric top squark and lightest neutralino contributes

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble collapse can be marked by an explosive growth in prices that suddenly ends at a potential critical point. The varied models also highlight how bubble parameters interact, influencing the likelihood of bubble survival despite expected negative market externalities. Notably, when considering the possibility of mixed expectations among market participants, the tendency for bubble collapse to be sudden is contingent upon specific economic conditions, pointing to a complex relationship between financial market behaviors and theoretical expectations.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying from zero to five times the angular frequency, or instantaneous driving forces that cycled between zero and four times the angular frequency, and the results were compared to constant driving scenarios.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments. Moreover, they tend to overlook the unique interaction between reviews and users/items when training a prediction model. In order to address these issues, a novel deep learning framework, called Sentiment Aware Interactive Recommendation (S AIR), is proposed. It consists of a user/item-based encoder, a review-based encoder, and a collaborative filter-based encoder, which are integrated through gate mechanisms to capture diverse representation. The obtained representations are then fed into a multi-task framework, including a low-rank matrix factorization task and a sentiment analysis task. The latter task informs the matrix factorization task with user/item embeddings reflecting their respective overall sentiments. The proposed framework, which is evaluated using real-world datasets, outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and explainability.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to create Dialectal Arabic-English CS text, exploring the impact of different techniques on resulting systems' performance and their consistency across different task tasks. Eight distinct data augmentation methods were tested, including replacement, copying, and combining methods with the top-performing ones selected for further examination. Notably, our best-performing system achieved a state-of-the-art result on the WikiCS task, outperforming previous best results by a significant margin of 3.5%. This study aims to contribute insights on utilizing data augmentation for improved CS NLP performance in future systems.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact open topology's inherited structure.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theories of conformal field theory, particularly those that yield sigma-models describing interactions between multiple strings. We're focusing on six-dimensional supersymmetric sigma-models with unique properties, like those involving non-supersymmetric surfaces and those that exhibit a specific type of symmetry, $Z_4$. By extending the established concept of geometric winding numbers, we've determined the possible forms that these D-branes can take. We're relating the points at which D-branes meet the center of the spectral problem to specific data called Thaddeees' near-horizon fields that occur at the edge of these D-branes. We're also connecting the behavior of the center vortices to the characteristics of the Thaddeees' near-horizon fields that occur away from the edge, thus establishing a relationship between the established concepts of the Thaddeees' construction and the new geometric interpretations of these D-branes that we discovered.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across domains, including engineering and computer graphics. A fundamental concept in addressing these challenges is the mesh, a composite of basic elements where hexahedral units offer enhanced computational advantages. However, mesh integrity relies on the quality of its components. The issue arises when elements take on shapes hindering precise calculations, rendering them unusable. To deliver accurate outcomes, it is crucial to correct such elements' morphology, rendering them valid. This study synthesizes the outcomes of two studies to develop a mesh assessment and correction framework. By combining their findings, we establish a functioning algorithm but also recognize its potential for enhancement, thus introducing multiple improvements to accelerate its processing speed and robustness. The resulting algorithm is subsequently compared with alternative methods through testing. This work presents a new efficient and reliable method to repair flawed meshes, facilitating optimal results for various applications.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably high precision, demonstrating an average error of less than 2% across an extensive range of technological parameters and output loads. As a result, the proposed model presents itself as a computationally efficient alternative for fast design iterations in CMOS inverter design.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
deriving policies from unpredictable function models. However, explicitly
calculating these policies is often impractical due to the high computational
requirements. A commonly used substitute for predicting policies directly is to
approximate a Q-function, but existing methods often lack theoretical guarantees
for policies derived from Q-functions. Our work provides theoretical assurances for
extracting policies from Q-functions learned through the use of neural networks,
without relying on noisy data. To facilitate this, we establish a guarantee for
polices derived from Q-functions, prove the reliability of Q-function-based
policies, and show the applicability of our method to a wide range of Q-function
approximators, including neural networks. Our method's practical effectiveness is
demonstrated by our results in continuous control scenarios for robots. Our code can be
found here: https://github.com/GregoryClimer/Lipschitz-Q.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data suggested distinct posterior regions associated with each. Consequently, our results supported the agency hypothesis over the visual feature hypothesis and revealed the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, with two superimposed patterns of animation.

In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, commonly used methods such as the finite element method and finite volume method are often prone to inaccuracies and artifacts like oscillations and spurious currents, especially when handling complex conditions. In our study, we explored an alternative approach, involving the integration of interpolated results from a thoroughly tested version of the theoretical model, in conjunction with an optimized method for solving partial differential equations called reduced order modeling. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach through the accurate reconstruction of fluctuation velocities, concentration profiles, and temperature distributions in scenarios involving rapid changes. Notably, our findings show that this approach can produce reliable results with a minimal number of observations, even when the problem is highly nonlinear and difficult to solve precisely.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV in the hard-intermediate state. Observations show the type C QPO frequency varied between 2.1 to 3.3 Hz, and then sharply increased to ~9 Hz. This phenomenon is associated with the evolution of corona size and feedback fraction. When correlated with radio observations, these findings suggest that the morphology of the corona might influence the formation of a jet in hard-intermediate states leading to the soft-intermediate state transition.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they might adapt training agents' behaviors instead of learning the task itself, resulting in poor performance when interacting with new agents during deployment. 

To address this issue, we suggest a new strategy, the Agent Transfer Evaluation Framework (ATEF), which allows you to assess MARL agents' ability to work with other agents at training time and measure their performance during deployment. AEF does this by creating a proxy environment that isolates the agents from one another, utilizing either zero-shot or pre-trained communication systems to replace missing partner information. Subsequently, AEF evaluates agents' performance within a reduced state-space created by a special wrapper that isolates their interactions. Through the AEF assessment, the AEF optimizes communication systems and selects the most suitable MARL agent based on its performance using the chosen proxy environment. To verify the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we conducted comprehensive experiments involving multi-agent cooperation and communication tasks on physical robots, demonstrating the potential benefits of utilizing AEF to improve MARL agent deployment.

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and 
approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and 
transferring similarities and transitions across materials and textures. 
MatSim enables one-shot learning, empowering the identification of any 
material regardless of the context or circumstances using only one or 
multiple examples. Visual material recognition is a crucial element in 
several industries such as food processing, agriculture, and industrial 
production. Our work involves leveraging vast resources commonly used 
by computer graphics artists to develop a CGI dataset centered around 
material similarity, incorporating physics-based rendering, varied 3D 
object assignments, and diverse environmental conditions to simulate 
real-world scenarios. To accommodate applications requiring a seamless 
transition between states or exposure to water, we also simulated more 
dynamic processes and liquid interactions. To ensure a smooth transition 
between states or exposure to water, we further simulated processes and 
created examples of material transformation. To advance One-Shot Learning 
and enable the transfer of knowledge across materials and scenarios, 
we established a research consisting of, thereby extending current 
machine learning techniques to accommodate additional input channels. 
Our research offers several visual material transformation examples, 
as well as a range of real-world images utilizing a similar approach 
to existing datasets MatSim has been released on GitHub along with 
corresponding code and demos on GitHub and Zeugma.ai.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by introducing four different types of Lie 2-algebras derived from 2-plectic manifolds, Courant algebroids, homotopy Poisson manifolds and multivector fields on a Lie groupoid. The Lie 2-algebra cohomology is also reintroduced and its lower-degree instances analyzed. The integration of strict Lie 2-algebras to strict Lie 2-groups is also a point of discussion in the paper.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we leverage self and cross attention mechanisms in the Transformer model to derive feature descriptors that are context-dependent for both images. This approach allows our method, known as LoFTR, to effectively find dense matches in low-texture regions that other methods struggle with, under diverse lighting conditions, without being affected by noise. Experiments on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin, particularly in indoor scenes. Additionally, our method outperforms existing techniques on OWID and AERIALVIEW datasets. Further details can be found on our project website.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and stellar variations. Secondly, by characterising local bias, they identify its causes and strategies to mitigate them. Thirdly, by examining stellar bias, they explore its relationships with magnetic activity, stellar properties, and spatial patterns on the disk and bolometric flux surface. Finally, they establish a framework for identifying and highlighting problematic regions within a dataset and suggest future research directions to alleviate the Bperp bias.

This research paper explores a pricing approach that motivates consumers to adapt their energy usage patterns by offering discounts for off-peak energy and higher rates during peak hours. A thorough examination of this policy is conducted through analysis and simulation, with a focus on understanding its effect on social welfare, fairness, and individual incentives within smart home environments. Our study draws upon real-world data from the Nils Krummenacher Smart Home dataset, enables us to compare simulated results with actual consumer responses to dynamic pricing.

The generalized form of the Einstein theory, the Rastall theory of gravity, incorporates the law of conservation of energy and momentum. We derive a charged black string solution using the Newman-Janis approach in a Rastall theory background. Next, we investigate thermodynamic properties, such as Hawking temperature, for these black strings and study their graphical representations with respect to event horizons. Additionally, we examine the impact of Rastall theory on Hawking temperature and assess the charged black string stability. Furthermore, taking quantum gravity effects into account, we investigate modified Hawking temperatures. We also explore the physical behavior of these black strings in the presence of quantum gravity and a spin parameter stemming from the Rastall theory.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in the Birkhoff theorem will be proportional to $t\mu_{\lambda=1}(x)$.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. These stars are rare and hard to locate, and our understanding of the halo of the Galaxy relies on the analysis of a limited number of metal-poor stars. New research has discovered nine metal-poor stars with low surface gravity, which were then studied using a high-powered telescope. The analysis of our own Galaxy's chemical composition suggests that the majority of metal-poor stars with low surface gravity reside in haloes at a distance of 15-32 kiloparsecs. We found that the frequency of these stars decreases slightly as their distance increases. Our research also indicates that the chemical composition of our own Galaxy's halo is composed of 62 +/- 8% from the halo population, 34 +/- 19% from the bulge population, and 4 +/- 19% from the thick disk population. Furthermore, our research found that the majority of metal-poor stars with low surface gravity have radial velocities consistent with isoradius contours and that our own Galaxy's halo population is part of a bar structure that forms stars with low surface gravity. Finally, our research revealed that the majority of metal-poor stars with low surface gravity have high internal kinematics and that our own Galaxy's halo population is part of a bar structure that forms stars with low surface gravity.

This research splits the Earth into a grid of hexagonal cells to collect and analyze worldwide data on daily temperature and precipitation records from over 42,000 stations. The study examines the date of the last winter snowmelt, defined as the last daily temperature above 10 degrees Celsius according to the Koppen climate classification, as a key indicator of seasonal trends. By employing techniques from information theory to analyze time series data, the researchers investigated changes in the frequency of seasonal patterns over the past six decades in regions all over the world. They discovered that the majority of regions have experienced shorter-than-average winter seasons, with approximately 70% experiencing last-winter snowmelt earlier than expected. In contrast, areas in the Northern Hemisphere that experience warm seasons in spring experienced later spring seasons, with about 70% experiencing spring seasons that have lasted less than usual. The analysis also showed that regions in the Southern Hemisphere that experience warm seasons in spring experienced later-than-expected last-spring snowmelt in autumn, with about 60% of these areas experiencing fall seasons that have lasted less than anticipated. The researchers found that regions in the Southern Hemisphere that experience warm seasons in fall experienced earlier-than-expected last-winter snowmelt in winter, with about 55% experiencing earlier-than-expected last-winter snowmelt in regions in the Northern Hemisphere. The study revealed that temperature trends are the main driver of seasonal changes, with temperature and precipitation records indicating that temperature trends have significantly accelerated over the study

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically to ascertain how they correlate with typological characteristics. This investigation seeks to answer whether these metrics assess the same underlying aspect of language or, alternatively, measure different facets of morphological complexity. The results from principal component analysis suggest that a substantial portion of variation across the eight measures is linearly associated.

Researchers at Meneghetti et al have discovered an increased occurrence of small gravitational lens effects, specifically caused by low-mass objects. To analyze the properties of these substructures, which cannot be directly observed, researchers turn to N-body simulations. These simulations show that early-type galaxies in the standard $\Lambda$CDM model develop more massive central objects and fewer satellite galaxies compared to observations. To resolve this discrepancy, researchers considered an early model of self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) as an alternative explanation. When applying this model to early-type galaxies in their sample, researchers found the predicted substructure density in line with the observed lens effects. The self-interacting cross-section required by the late-time galaxy rotation curves was found to be consistent with the earlier measurements, indicating that self-interacting dark matter can potentially resolve both the standard $\Lambda$CDM model's inconsistencies with respect to lensing and substructure density.

This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by creating an approximation space for the solutions based on two sources of information: X, the initial data set, and Y, the output data set. Our goal is to minimize the approximation error by identifying a subspace in the Galerkin method for PPDEs. Due to the lack of exact models, we resort to Bayesian approximation theory to develop an algorithm that combines sampling from the posterior distribution and local optimization to find an optimal approximation space. This approach can be applied to various types of approximation problems and is demonstrated using unit disc wave and parabolic PPDEs in the study. Moreover, our method has the advantage of providing uncertainty estimates in the approximation process.

This research introduces m-arcsaturation-based versions of the well-known FastICA methods in the presence of probable data. The proposed m-arcsaturation-based FastICA techniques employ a novel activation function developed from an analytical expression of the Maximum Likelihood estimator, using a probability distribution model that accurately represents random data. The proposed approaches offer flexible operations between continuous and binary representations, are suitable for large datasets, and can be applied to feature extraction tasks, including dimensionality reduction, clustering, and independent component separation. Using the Sum of Gaussian noise model, the results demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve higher precision, precision stability, and accuracy compared to the original FastICA and other established methods, such as the FastICA (t-tailed), flexible ICA, and Generalized FastICA. Furthermore, experimental evaluations verify the effectiveness of the proposed methods on various real-world datasets, showing significant performance improvements.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. It addresses spatial resolution ambiguity through a quad-tree based method that segmentates regions based on data density, and uses statistical analysis incorporating the Poisson distribution to highlight anomalies in post density. Furthermore, event duration is determined by evaluating content similarity and incorporating user feedback to accommodate data scarcity during initial phases. Two case studies were conducted to demonstrate the efficacy of this framework: one focusing on general user-generated data and another on Twitter data specifically, including a comparison of our approach with existing algorithms using user-generated data and existing event detection methods across multiple platforms. The results showed that our proposed framework outperformed the competitors in event detection, and we observed that our method can accommodate unpredictable user behavior and real-time data fluctuations.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for the measure-valued elliptic PDE $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ within a smooth domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Here, $\Gamma$ represents a $C^{1,\alpha}$-smooth hypersurface, with $Q$ defined as a $C^{0,\alpha}$ density on $\Gamma$, and $A$ characterizes a symmetric, uniformly elliptic and $W^{1,q}$-regular tensor $(q > n)$. Furthermore, the article examines the optimality of these conditions applied to the problem parameters $A$ and $Q$.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth and transition metal alloys achieve high magnetization due to high transition metal content. By utilizing computational searches based on fundamental laws, researchers predicted 37 cobalt-rich compounds, specifically 17 YCo$_{16}$ and 20 YCo$_{20}$, which were identified as stable with a high likelihood. These cobalt-rich alloys were discovered to exhibit increased phase stability at elevated temperatures, attributed to increased vibrational entropy. Notably, YCo$_{16}$ and YCo$_{20}$ displayed enhanced magnetization and Curie temperatures compared to the extensively studied compound Y$_{2}$Co$_{17}$, specifically 0.22 T and 204 K for YCo$_{16}$, and 0.29 T and 204 K for YCo$_{20}$.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids typically based on the value of the ad impression and optimal bid price. Nevertheless, existing bidding strategies often overlook the randomness of user behaviors, such as click-through rates, and the uncertainty surrounding costs resulting from auction competition. In our study, we explicitly take into account the uncertainty associated with estimated ad impression values and the risk tolerance of a DSP under specific conditions via a sequential decision-making process. A novel bidding algorithm, grounded in reinforcement learning and incorporating budget constraints, is introduced to address this issue for the first time, integrating both estimation uncertainty and the dynamic risk tolerance of a DSP. We have mathematically demonstrated the intrinsic relationship between uncertainty and risk tolerance based on the value-at-risk metric. Two distinct formulations for modeling risk tolerance are then presented: a rule-based model founded on three essential properties, and an adaptive learning method built on self-supervised reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments conducted using public datasets demonstrate the proposed framework outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in real-world scenarios.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the local unitary transformation of a shared state held by Alice and Bob. Specifically, the researchers examined the effect of local applications on the Wigner function of the combined state. They observed that Wigner negativity arises when Alice's state exhibits quantum steering power. Furthermore, the smallest marginal density matrix infimum cannot serve as an indicator for Wigner negativity. Nonetheless, certain conditions related to the infimum of norms from side-information can signal Wigner negativity.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, yet the impact of random number seed non-uniformity on these systems has not been thoroughly investigated. Despite the effectiveness of the fast Fourier transform method in correcting non-uniformity, this study demonstrates that it also introduces new uncertainties under collective attacks. The research employs both theoretical and simulated data to examine two scenarios: non-gaussian privacy amplification and non-uniformity, and quantum key generation with non-uniformity alone. The findings show that non-uniformity can broaden the secure data rate interval, but it also accelerates the depletion of secure data rates. The study further reveals that simulated results match theoretical predictions, and simulated data without noise can perfectly satisfy the theoretical secure boundary, but the presence of real noise in the simulation can cause it to expand beyond the theoretical secure boundary, and simulated data rates are nearly 20% lower than the theoretical rate due to real noise interfering in the random number generation process.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

We'll examine the diffusion process described by the equation $u_t(t, x) =
\tfrac{1}{2}\{x u(t, x)\}_{xx} - \alpha \{x u(t, x)\}_{x}$ with $u(0, x) =
\delta(x - x_0)$ for $t, x, \alpha \ge 0$, initially derived and solved by Feller
for modeling independently reproducing population growth, focusing on related
coalescent processes. We derive the probability distribution for $A_n(s, t)$,
which denotes the number of ancestors at time $s$ in the past of a sample of size
$n$ from the population at time $t$. This leads to two practical applications:
efficient calculation of stationary sampling distributions in subcritical multi-type
populations and constructing a coalescent tree for supercritical populations,
yielding sampling distributions for populations that follow the multi-locus
neutral model.

In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems with a particular focus on systems utilizing delayed coherent quantum feedback. By using a specific mathematical approach within the rotating wave approximation, we demonstrate that N-photon scattering matrices in single-qubit systems can be expressed as a combination of (N-1) photon effective vertex functions. Additionally, we derive a comprehensive set of equations that govern these vertex functions. One advantage of this approach is its versatility in handling problems with multiple radiation channels, regardless of bandwidth, mode dispersion, or interaction structure. Our method also allows us to study complex multi-photon scattering problems that cannot be solved using traditional methods. Furthermore, we extend this technique to more complex systems involving multiple emitters by providing an exact set of equations for two and three-photon scattering operators. This theoretical framework is applied to a specific example: the experimental study of three-photon scattering on a giant acoustic atom, reported in [Nat. Phys. 15, 1123 (2019)].

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter is by utilizing boosted dark matter interactions. The framework for light dark matter interactions involving no spin is complex and has few theoretical predictions available. The situation becomes more complex when considering that the light dark matter is moving rapidly, resulting in an added complication of relativistic factors. Our focus will be on how spin-dependent scattering affects the effective operators in a model where dark matter interacts with standard model particles. The Scattering Length Formalism has been established as a reliable method for calculating this interaction; however, this approach only works in the non-relativistic context and needs modification to apply to the boosted scenario. The study of the proton structure factor, which varies with energy, is particularly interesting as this is a key component in studying solar system movements and galaxy clustering. Our findings reveal that for boosted dark matter, this interaction is not merely increased but rather amplified depending on the time component, with a potential 20-fold increase predicted. The time component-related effect is anticipated to be more prominent in the early solar system and on short-term predictions of planet motion. The study of kl and f17 terms, which involve a low-kinetic model used for boosted dark matter, showed that these too have relativistic corrections. The analysis further discovered coupling combinations that are not forbidden by existing constraints to still be able to meet present day direct detection requirements and at the same time satisfy requirements for the solar system's dynamics. Our findings show that what initially seemed a minor effect could actually
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the calculation of a phase difference between successive symbols and frames. In phase modulation systems, the second-order differential detection method outperforms other coherent and non-coherent detection techniques in terms of bit error rate when receiving a infinite number of bits. Notably, conventional second-order differential detection has a significant drawback - it severely reduces data transfer rates. In this research, new effective minimum mean Square Error (MSE) detectors are presented, designed to surpass conventional second-order differential detection in performance and minimize data transfer rate loss, while also being simpler to implement and allowing faster modulation speeds. MSE-based codebooks are developed to facilitate the design of these optimal detectors, which can then be approximated by lower-complexity detectors, such as least squares (LS) and conventional differential detection. In practical applications, these sub-optimal detectors can provide better overall system performance, even when subjected to frequent variations in carrier phase, such as in mobile communications.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To make this framework more practical, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to assign labels and demonstrate that the suggested methodology effectively utilizes human time, as demonstrated on three simulated environments and the MineCraft world.

We're exploring nucleon structure functions within noncommutative space-time, with the aim of uncovering the internal makeup of nucleons. To do this, we're utilizing corrected and novel vertices that arise from noncommutativity, and we're expressing the proton's structure functions using the noncommutative tensor \theta_{\mu\nu}.

In typical topological systems, significant disruptions trigger a phase shift, but we have developed an adjustable version of the Toric code that remains stable under even extreme external influences, characterized by a "critical line" where no phase shift occurs, and remains stable for arbitrary strong interactions. Notably, this outcome is facilitated by incorporating an arbitrary strong interaction term between adjacent qubits and demonstrates the ability to protect topological properties through a balance of energy scale and fractal-like structure known as a "butterfly network".

We investigate the eigenspectra of large, randomly constructed Hermitian block matrices, whose structure is perturbed by a finite rank complex modification. Given that the band's width expands faster than the square root of the matrix's size, our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of the imaginary components of the eigenvectors aligns with the results from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This finding was achieved using the methods and approaches developed in the arXiv paper, 1802.03813.

Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained models leveraging abstract meaning representations of sentences, thereby gaining deeper semantic understanding enabling them to excel in various dialogue-related tasks. Nevertheless, applying these models to dialogue data is hindered by a lack of sufficient training data featuring the abstract meaning representations. In a bid to overcome this obstacle, this study introduces a new pre-training approach that combines language models with a novel text augmentation technique that makes use of semantic information from abstract meaning representations, thereby allowing the model to learn semantic traits during the training process. Furthermore, this study develops a new task that makes use of semantic information from abstract meaning representations to guide response generation. Results from both experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in dialogue generation tasks.

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on principles from programming languages and learning theory to establish a comprehensive framework for assessing interpretability. This proposed method captures the essence of how a person learns an algorithm, and through rigorous evaluation, we prove its advantages in four key areas - it applies universally, can be computed easily, yields distinct results, and accurately tracks increasing complexity. By presenting the framework through a hypothetical scenario and elaborating its foundational concepts, we highlight the practical applications of this measurement tool, notably for those responsible for choosing between algorithms based on their merits.

Anomaly detection without labelled data is increasingly being used to identify unusual patterns within datasets, given that manually annotating data can be impractical or costly; one such unsupervised method that has gained popularity in recent times is the Isolation Forest algorithm, which is known to be efficient. Nevertheless, a variant of this method, utilizing the assistance of unlabelled data via weak supervision, is still an underdeveloped area. In response to this, our novel unsupervised Isolation Forest-based approach employs weak supervision to determine anomaly scores, before identifying the data points representing the anomalous class. Ultimately, our weak-specified Isolation Forest method exhibits improved clarity in classifying anomalies, when compared to the standard Isolation Forest method that relies solely on unlabelled data; interestingly, our approach is also superior to other weak-specified models, showcasing its unique capacity for accurate anomaly detection.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point. To maximize average cross-sectional area, any perpendicular section must contain the centroid of the shape. Additionally, to facilitate a general solution, we assume a shape confined within a square boundary. It becomes necessary to express the average cross-section through a point in mathematical terms and to establish constraints ensuring the existence of a unique solution. These constraints are most demanding when the point lies on the square's edge, requiring a linear solution in this scenario. However, when the point resides inside the square, the average cross-section's optimal value can be determined using a quadratic formula, which also provides the coefficient of variation. These results can be applied across various practical applications, including the design of steel sections. Moreover, we illustrate the theoretical findings with several numerical examples.

There's been a shift in natural language understanding research from isolated tasks 
to more general applications, such as commonsense reasoning, which requires massive 
collections of annotated knowledge to be effective. To meet this demand, we've been 
working on expanding the Atlas of Life Knowledge (ALK), a extensively curated 
common sense knowledge graph with over a million entries, to incorporate new entities 
and relationships that were previously unknown. To achieve this, we've developed a 
state-of-the-art data expansion method, which seamlessly integrates external knowledge 
sources like Wikipedia and ConceptNet without needing label annotations. By merging these 
entities and relationships under a unified schema, we've significantly expanded the 
scope of ALK, increasing its knowledge entities by over 300%. Our results, which have 
been validated across three distinct metrics, clearly demonstrate the benefits of our 
method, allowing us to confidently include new knowledge and ensure it aligns with what 
already exists. The expanded Atlas of Life Knowledge is accessible at: https://alk.gptg.to/.

We introduce the data reduction and processing strategy for the Hi-GAL survey. This protocol is part of the Second Herschel Survey project, focusing on thorough, massive, and uniform observations of the Galactic plane using Hi-Res Spectroscopic Survey of the Galactic plane (Hi-SPEC) as a companion programme. All Hi-SPEC details are incorporated into the pipeline for its spectral data. The pipeline consists of four main steps - an independent assessment of pipeline validity through Hi-SPEC's data, thorough quality control of science data through various diagnostic tests, accurate calibration of science data using established methods, and comprehensive data processing through an established method. The pipeline is available at www.sharc.net/herschel-hi-gal. All Hi-GAL data, including the Hi-SPEC spectra, will be released through the Herschel Archive alongside the archive's full processing. This release, alongside the Hi-SPEC data release, will also encompass a comprehensive data quality document. The pipeline's efficiency was evaluated using Hi-SPEC's test fields, and its performance on the full survey is demonstrated using one of the Hi-SPEC fields. The document includes detailed descriptions of the Hi-SPEC data reduction, Hi-SPEC's data processing strategy and a comprehensive description of the Hi-GAL observational properties. The document is available online through www.sharc.net/herschel-hi-gal.

Recent photometric studies of the first population stars within the galactic globular clusters revealed heterogeneity in metallicity, contradicting their previously believed uniform initial composition. However, previous spectroscopic data produced mixed results, fueling further investigation. A thorough high-resolution analysis was conducted on five bright red giant stars within the NGC 2808 cluster, using atmospheric parameters sourced from the literature and resulting in precise iron, silicon, calcium, titanium, and nickel abundance measurements with low margins of error. Despite minimal uncertainties, these targeted stars demonstrated a notable 0.25 dex range of iron content. Probing further, these iron levels directly correlated with spatial location within the cluster, alongside variation in helium content and photometric measures. Notably, relative abundance ratios of valued elements exhibited low variation. A detailed examination and in-depth discussion of these findings were then conducted, seeking understanding of these observed disparities among the cluster's stars.

To facilitate a deeper understanding of one-dimensional physical systems, we consider a simplified single file model. We derive an analytical solution for the complete first exit time statistics of an overdamped single file with absorbing boundary conditions, after which we apply these findings to investigate the speed-accuracy relationship, examining how this property is influenced by the mean squared displacement and the entropic repulsive forces within the system.

Quantum Mechanics contradicts the universally assumed, classical cause-and-effect relationship established by Bayes' rule in physics. While believed to hold for all processes, Bayes' rule leads to inconsistencies in Quantum Mechanics when applied to certain situations such as Frauchiger-Renner's paradox. Similar issues also occur in the Hardy setup, despite treating Quantum Mechanics as a non-local theory. To resolve these inconsistencies, an input-output causal relation, based on a modified version called quantum Bayes' rule, is introduced, applicable to quantum processes including coherent superpositions and nonlocal correlations. Quantum Bayes' rule resolves the contradictions in the mentioned thought experiments, confirming the consistency of Quantum Mechanics with its own principles.

We initially report findings regarding corrections to system size for the state equation, trace anomaly, and speed of sound, using two specific theoretical frameworks: a model for massless scalar fields and another based on quenched QCD, both applying periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we share ongoing results involving the application of Dirichlet boundary conditions to quenched QCD.

Let $F_2$ be the prime field consisting of two elements. The general linear group of rank $s$, denoted as $GL_s(F_2)$, represents the group of invertible matrices with rank $s$ over $F_2$. A specific subspace within the Steenrod algebra, denoted as $\Lambda_{2}\left\{s\right\}$, consists of a combination of rank $s$ over $F_2$. The algebraic transfer homomorphism $\xi_{A,s}: \text{Ext}^{s,(s-1)}A_{*}(2)\rightarrow\text{Ext}^{s,(1)}A_{*}(2)$, where $(s-1)$ and $(1)$ indicate the degree of operations, and $A_{*}(2)$ is the Steenrod algebra, which has been studied by the mathematicians in this field. The work presents an alternate demonstration of the isomorphism $\xi_{A,s}$ by developing a specific model using a combination of a free prop and a graph Prop, which is a mathematical algebraic system. The resulting model has been shown to be useful in constructing an inverse of the isomorphism $\xi_{A

Astronomers observing far ultraviolet wavelengths from Earth's orbit have been hindered by a bright signal due to geocoronal radiation, making it difficult to obtain accurate readings of celestial objects in this range. Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Rocket Group are developing an innovation that can filter out this unwanted radiation, enabling high-quality far ultraviolet observations of space objects. The radiation's spectrum spans certain wavelengths, and by using a filter with specific absorptions, it can be blocked, allowing scientists to study objects in space more precisely. The team is creating a device utilizing atomic hydrogen that can absorb and filter out the radiation, and has refined its design based on initial simulations of the radiation's effects.

Optimal distributed controller design under communication limitations is 
a challenge that a new class of systems, graph symmetric systems, helps to 
address. Graph symmetry offers a convenient way to encapsulate structural 
information about these systems, which in turn enables researchers to leverage 
this structure to develop decentralized control strategies. A new approach 
is introduced to obtain optimal distributed control, which identifies the 
suboptimal control operator through spectral analysis of a modified system 
operator that incorporates communication limitations. A key property of 
optimalness is established, along with a criterion to determine if a 
suboptimal control is optimal, which can be verified through the evaluation 
of a specific function and its associated Hessian matrix, which is also 
bounded by a Kronecker product of two matrix norms. A set of preconditioning 
techniques, which include Max-Min, Min-Min, and Power methods, are also 
developed to reduce the computational complexity associated with these methods, 
which in turn enables researchers to determine the optimal function value and 
an associated suboptimal control operator, which is bounded by a specific 
norm. A set of supported theorems also demonstrate the consistency and 
convergence of these methods, which also lies on the structural information of 
the system, which in turn explains the ability of these methods to achieve 
convergence.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a representation's loss in quality due to transformations. It achieves this through a balance of precision and efficiency by storing the most informative image variations during the indexing process. Experimental results demonstrate that active indexing yields superior search performance, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art results, and significantly outperforms passive strategies, improving the speed by 10 to 60 times while retaining 85% of the precision.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an eavesdropping channel must
not be a direct line connection to the main communication channel. Furthermore,
we investigate how a sender can securely transmit one message to a recipient,
while an adversary attempts to guess the message, finding that authenticating one
message is more feasible than multiple messages, and requires significantly
more channel strength for an extension of the extended authenticated coding
problem.

Reevaluating the running Brownian particle under a constant force requires a more intricate approach than previously thought. While it's commonly believed that the particle immediately enters a stable running state, our thorough analysis reveals this isn't the case. In fact, after applying the force, the particle undergoes damped oscillations around its resting point before eventually escaping to the running state through a complex dynamics influenced by several factors, including a non-linear rest position and a critical force threshold. The exact mathematical equations governing this transition are incredibly challenging to solve, necessitating a deeper numerical exploration of the particle's dynamics. Our in-depth study not only sheds light on the origin of the running state but also uncovers other important aspects, such as how the particle's motion changes when its motion is monitored and influenced by the resulting periodic oscillations.

Studies examining the effects of fiscal shocks often fail to account for varying economic conditions, assuming a one-size-fits-all model. This work uses a data-driven method to address this issue by incorporating a variety of features into a time-varying multiplier model. An important discovery was that the sign of the multiplier depends on whether the economy is experiencing growth or contraction, as well as the duration since the Great Financial Crisis. An initial expansionary shock has a positive effect during a recession but a negative effect during a boom. Conversely, a contractionary shock has the opposite impact when compared to an equivalent expansionary shock. This research also discovered that the multipliers associated with government and private spending exhibit different characteristics, and that a novel feature extraction method can be utilized to support the finding that the Giavazzi and Misala effect is predominantly influenced by the change in business confidence.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to photons in the vacuum that emit an energy back to the charge in proportion to n^2, a greater increase than that of the -2n\hbar of a charge in a Landau level.

The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, often exceeding hundreds, by considering the context of each mention.
