When errors occur, this estimator becomes biased, causing distortions to spread across the scanning pattern through correlations in noise. A notable effect of this phenomenon is the creation of 'X' shapes surrounding strong point sources in typical scanning patterns. This paper examines why such distortion occurs and introduces both established and novel techniques for mitigating or eliminating the effects of spherically symmetric instrumental pointing errors, with a focus on how these effects relate to the CMB Secondary Anisotropy package.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by referential ambiguity, limiting the scope of applications for instruction-based learning algorithms. In our research, we address this issue by redefining the teaching process as a reference-resolution task, drawing on cognitive theories to predict the teacher's intent. Specifically, we implement a'most similar' reference-resolution strategy, evaluating the similarity between object representations rather than instructions. While directly using similarity metrics can lead to inaccurate results, we overcome this limitation by pre-training our object representations using a variety of instruction-related attributes. We test our proposed method across multiple domains and learnings, demonstrating its effectiveness in resolving referential ambiguity and achieving improved instruction following.

Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, specifically in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of extracting crucial state information using only polynomially increasing measurements. This study brings the concepts of shadow tomography and quantum channel state discrimination together, introducing a novel framework, called channel shadow estimation, to effectively predict a quantum channel's outputs without full process measurement. This approach leverages prior knowledge of a quantum channel, obtained from prior process measurements, to produce accurate predictions of the channel's inputs, eventually leading to accurate determinations of the full process. This method's performance is examined through the practical application of channel shadow estimation to quantum control, specifically in the accurate determination of unknown magnetic field strengths.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures via a novel formula, as well as generalising the Minkowski inequality, with equality occurring when the specified constants are maximally disparate. Additionally, we examine how the Cheeger constant compares across different sets, including subsets and supersets, particularly when these sets have smooth boundaries. Our analysis also involves deriving new comparisons among other important geometric parameters such as the projection depth, width of the tangent path and radius of tangency. Furthermore, we introduce a novel formula expressing the radius of tangency in terms of the Cheeger constant, along with generalising a key result on Bubers' comparison principle. Our study focuses on planar convex bodies, but we also extend our findings to numerical, approximated versions of these sets, which are essential in computational geometry and statistics. Our work is largely self-contained and provides an in-depth review of relevant theories, serving as a accessible entry point to the research subject for readers without prior knowledge.

The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) holds great potential for transforming communications systems. By harnessing their adaptability and swift deployment capabilities, it becomes feasible to supply content in densely populated areas or regions lacking essential infrastructure. In this study, we explore a UAV model that serves a maximum number of users at various locations within a set time frame. To achieve optimal trajectory planning, we develop a mixed-integer linear program for problem formulation. For large-scale problems involving a staggering number of trajectory options, we establish a link to the orienteering problem, subsequently proposing an efficient greedy algorithm. Simulation results validate the efficacy and rapidity of this proposed algorithm, yielding solutions comparable to the optimal outcomes. Consequently, this approach can be utilized for planning strategic content caching and UAV trajectory optimization.

The low-energy electronic properties of bilayer graphene can be described by a two-valley model due to its approximately conical band structure. High-energy interactions are known to contribute a linear energy term, forcing the valleys to remain equal in energy. At low energies, short-range interactions take over, causing the valleys to become unequal in energy and generating a valley-dependent hopping parameter. Using the density matrix renormalization group method, we study the effects of these short-range interactions on the drain of heat in bilayer graphene. A new frequency-dependent Drude weight is introduced and found to be highly variable with respect to frequency. This result suggests that, in certain cases, the drainage of heat can be significantly slowed down. Our findings also imply that, in order to control thermal conduction within bilayer graphene, one may utilize a gate voltage to adjust the effective short-range interaction strength.

The conformation of surface molecules greatly affects their functions on materials' surface. For Sc2TbN@C80, changes in its structure, which occurs when heated, not only alter its molecular composition but also shift the positions of the molecules' orbits and charge states. In this study, DFT calculations revealed that warming the molecule causes its outer shell to expand, which in turn increases the workfunction of the material. Notably, the expansion of the outer shell is associated with a molecular debate over symmetry. While the Tobium nitrogen double bond maintains the molecule's symmetry, the presence of quadruplet spin and lobes around the axis suggests otherwise. Furthermore, the structure of the molecule's outer shell can be visualized using B3U-Map, a molecular analysis tool.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets, traditionally unlinked to the internet, at an exponentially growing pace. Data security and user privacy concerns loom large over the IoT landscape, where devices operate on low power. Conventional encryption methods are unsuitable for these devices, necessitating a need for contemporary lightweight algorithms tailored for IoT settings, which this communication seeks to summarize.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau$. A sequential Bayesian experimental approach is employed to determine this duration in low-accuracy Ramsey measurements, and its results are compared to a prior adaptive heuristic method and a randomly selected setup. An efficient process that enables simultaneous measurement-taking and design calculations greatly minimizes the computational overhead associated with measurement time. When the precession frequency is the sole parameter being estimated, the Bayesian method exhibits significant improvements over the adaptive heuristic and random protocols, resulting in computation time savings of two and four times, respectively.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's tendency to lie close to shortest paths within its surrounding area. The Gromov centrality metric gauges importance at different network scales based on the size of the neighborhood and recovers well-known metrics as limiting cases. It is demonstrated that the Gromov centrality is sensitive to geometric and boundary constraints of the network, enabling the identification of various node types within random and real-world networks.

From a purely non-relativistic perspective, we derive the Poisson equation solution for empty space in a scenario with a rotating gravitational system, analogous to the Sun, and consider the case where a planet, treated as a point particle, interacts with the resulting gravitational field. Two mathematical approaches are taken to examine the effects of this system: analysis of the gravitational field, algebraic in nature, and study of the associated Hamiltonian, which requires knowledge of both position and velocity constraints for the planet. Three key findings emerge: first, the solution to the Poisson equation provides an accurate description of the gravitational field; second, application of the Schwarzschild metric is unnecessary for explaining phenomena such as the Kepler parabola; third, incorporation of special relativistic corrections reveals a more complex behavior, suggesting that the precession of Mercury's perihelion may be attributed to the properties of the azimuthally symmetric gravitational field rather than General Relativity.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, relating to matrices under similarity transformations. Despite substantial research on the topology of bundles of matrix pencils, some key issues remain unresolved. In particular, open questions include characterizing closure inclusions among bundles and determining whether these bundles are open within their own closures. This paper addresses these queries, revisiting existing notions and offering new insights through examples and counterexamples. Additionally, it outlines connections between these issues and well-established geometric concepts such as projective transformation, embedding, and morphisms between varieties.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds in detail, providing clear explanations of key concepts including solvmanifolds, nilmanifolds, and torus bundles. A brief overview of nilpotent Lie groups and solvable Lie algebras is also provided. Ultimately, we demonstrate that general topological spaces can be represented as a direct limit of solvmanifolds, allowing the algebraic framework of commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action to effectively model a wide range of T-dualities.

Cohen-Addad, Filtser, Klein, and Le created a stochastic graph embedding method in their FOCS '20 work that allowed minor-free graphs with diameter $D$ to be embedded into graphs with treewidth $O_{\epsilon}(\log n)$ with expected distortion $+\epsilon D$. The researchers later employed this method in their STOC '21 work to create a QPTAS for minor-free graphs. Filtser and Le developed a QPTAS for minor-free graphs with Baker's metric using a different approach in their STOC '21 work. The current research develops a new embedding method that reduces the treewidth to $O_{\epsilon}(\log\log n)$ while maintaining the previous distortion. As a result, the capacitated vehicle routing problem is resolved using a QPTAS, as it is a minor-free graph problem, but the space requirement is lowered to $O( n)$ bits. The researchers also discovered that the vehicle routing problem is solvable using a QPTAS when the vehicle capacity is bounded, as it is a minor-free graph problem, but the previous result uses $O( n^2 )$ bits of space. Moreover, the researchers created an efficient randomized algorithm that solves the $k$-Route-Rooted Spanning Tree problem in minor-free graphs with bounded tree path length $P$. The new algorithm runs in $O(PT)$ time and $O( n )$ space, as it is

For continuous dynamical systems, there exists a comprehensive study on the long-term behavior of certain types of strongly monotone systems.  Despite this, there have been fewer studies on the long-term behavior of discrete dynamical systems.  Research conducted by N.M. Macedo highlighted the uniqueness of the limit set of C1-smooth, strongly monotone discrete-time dynamical systems.  Inspired by this, we have expanded her findings, revealing that for a broad category of discrete-time dynamical systems, including those considered non-compact and with strongly monotone characteristics, the limit set is uniquely defined and consists of a single point or is empty.  Additionally, we have established the existence of orbit-limit trajectories for this category of discrete-time dynamical systems.

The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an ansatz using a shallow quantum circuit is key to successful simulations. Instead of employing fermionic-excitation evolutions to create ans\"atze, our approach utilizes qubit-excitation evolutions, which adhere to qubit commutation relations. By doing so, qubit excitation evolutions can accurately construct ans\"atze, even with a few gates, making them more efficient than fermionic-excitation evolutions. To take advantage of qubit excitation evolutions, we present the QEB-ADAPT-VQE protocol, which is an adaptive modification of the ADAPT-VQE. This new protocol iteratively appends evolutions of qubit excitation operators to a problem-tailored ansatz. Our results, obtained from benchmarking the QEB-ADAPT-VQE on small molecules, demonstrate that it surpasses both the fermionic-ADAPT-VQE and qubit-ADAPT-VQE in terms of circuit efficiency and convergence rate. Notably, our QEB-ADAPT-VQE outperforms the previously most efficient scalable VQE protocol, qubit-ADAPT-VQE.

A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of representation, its distribution, and a neural network mapping, with techniques like variational autoencoders (VAEs) often applied, but posing significant optimization challenges. Specifically, the inclusion of an encoder introduces complexity, particularly in terms of the amortization gap and the uncertainty of the variational approximation. Furthermore, the balance between objective function terms can critically impact model performance. Given these complexities, a simpler model, the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), which finds representations and their distribution by directly maximizing the model likelihood, is explored. By removing the need for an encoder, the DGD proves more efficient and effective than the VAE on several benchmarks, particularly in terms of optimization speed and robustness. The DGD also often outperforms the VAE in terms of the quality of generated samples, with the benefit of being easier to use and train. Ultimately, the DGD provides a useful baseline for researchers working with deep generative models.

The discovery of a common-spectrum process in recent NANOGrav findings has led to theories suggesting it could be evidence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) that exceeds expectations based on standard inflation combined with LCDM. If the SGWB exists and is amplified as predicted by the standard inflation + stiff inflation model, which combines LCDM, or by other possible inflation models that predict gravitational waves, this would have significant impacts on the expansion history of the universe, potentially resolving several long-standing cosmological problems. The standard inflation + stiff inflation model, which was previously believed to be discredited due to arguments based on perturbative incompatibility, is now reconsidered as a possible explanation for the observed tension between early and late-universe measurements of the Hubble constant, the cosmological power spectrum, and the estimated age of the universe. The proposed models require further development to provide a more detailed explanation for the observed data.

Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a comet's volatile substances. We utilized standalone observations with the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) of the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) of the comet C/2015 ER61, conducted shortly after its significant April outburst in 2017. The data collected on April 11 and 15 for HCN, CS, CH3OH, H2CO, HNC, and NH2CHO, alongside thermal emissions like ground-persistent and volatile flux, are reported here. The data shows that the emitted light originated primarily from the comet's inner region and that CS and HCN detected the deepest layers closest to the nucleus. The CS and HCN emission maps are analyzed at 28-29 and 32-33 GHz respectively, with the uncertainty of the origin of the detected lines yet to be determined. The data, a result of the large fluctuation in the ACA's pointing accuracy, may have introduced a large error. The data is therefore transformed to the scale of millibarns, rather than barns, to account for the uncertainty, with the information being compared to other comet models for evaluation.

We've developed a novel method for unsupervised speech synthesis, leveraging only speech data without requiring annotations for prosody, and thereby bypassing the need for transcription. This approach is built on three key elements: a voice encoder drawn from natural speech variations, a text encoder tied to a synthetic neural voice, and a speech decoder that combines the two encoders to produce spoken words. As our system relies entirely on unlabelled data for both training and evaluation, cross-entropy loss can only be calculated after the system is fully trained. Consequently, we employ a two-stage process where the voice and text encoders are initially trained, followed by the inclusion of the speech decoder. This sequence allows for the detection of the voice synthesis space through unsupervised means. We've found that our unsupervised approach yields comparable quality to supervised methods as measured by the average mean opinion score.

In an earlier paper, we analyzed quantum gravity models with specific lower bound assumptions in the spatially flat FLRW metric, leading to a minuscule universe at the Planck scale. However, in this current paper, we examine if there are other lower bound assumptions that might avoid the universe becoming too empty. Initially, we explore quadratic gravity, which incorporates a fraction of $\Lambda/3$ into the fractional energy density $\rho$, but we find that avoiding the empty universe requires an impractically small and dynamically unstable state. Subsequently, in models with non-abelian vector fields, $B_{\mu\nu}\wedge B^{†}_{\mu\nu}$ also contributes to the fractional energy density, but similarly, avoiding the empty universe demands an imperceptibly small and unstable state. Consequently, we conclude the universe cannot avoid becoming too empty based solely on these lower bound assumptions in the quadratic and non-abelian vector field gravity models.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notable instances including the adaptation of mixed-integer non-linear models to generate sustainable fuel alternatives. A novel approach, combining multi-criteria branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, is proposed for approximating Pareto fronts for such problems. A case study with realistic constraints on resource availability is presented, demonstrating that this proposed hybrid approach, with a dedicated evaluator, surpasses standalone non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2 in obtaining high-quality solutions within a set timeframe.

We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid.

The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding holistic workflows in cyberinfrastructures, allowing for deployment on virtual machines via cloud services such as JetStream. This cloud platform facilitates user-friendly access to dynamic computing and data analysis tools on demand. Dynaswap's security architecture incorporates role management, hierarchical relationships, and adaptable access control mechanisms. By integrating cutting-edge frameworks like Authentication-Authorization-Accounting and Blockchain technology, as well as advanced security features, Dynaswap provides a comprehensive protection system. Currently, the Dynaswap architecture is being validated in life-science research and educational settings within the Health Informatics field.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of reviews lack explicit opinion words, yet clearly convey human-aware sentiment, classified as implicit sentiment. Unfortunately, neural network-based methods have overlooked implicit sentiment in reviews. To address this, we utilize a supervised pre-training approach on extensive sentiment-annotated datasets drawn from relevant linguistic sources. By aligning implicit sentiment phrases with their matching sentiment labels, this pre-training method significantly improves the capture of both explicit and implicit sentiment orientations in reviews towards specific aspects. Our technique exhibits superior performance on the SemEval 2014 benchmarks and an in-depth examination demonstrates its effectiveness in extracting implicit sentiment.

We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control sampling affects logistic regression parameters related to a secondary outcome of interest. This is particularly significant when conducting mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in stratified case-control studies. Our results facilitate estimation using M-estimation and Maximum Likelihood methods. A simulation in a German dataset shows that our method yields accurate estimators, perform comparably to those from stratified weighted logistic regression, both when the confounding variables are binary and when they have multiple values.

This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under constraints for the base station's power output, RIS element constraints, and RIS phase shift limitations.
A problem that combines optimization and discrete variable management is proposed, which can be broken down into two separate issues due to the combination of continuous and integer variables.
A first solution employs the ANT COL COL algorithm, while a second solution combines the YALMIP tool with a reinforcement learning method, utilizing a collaborative agent to alternately address the two separate problems.
Results indicate that the proposed algorithms outperform traditional methods like the SumSecPower, MinSumSecPower, and Grouping-Based methods in terms of overall secrecy rate performance.

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that reprocesses perception data through a review of past experiences in order to minimize prediction errors. This idea becomes practical due to the incorporation of a memory mechanism and a pre-trained neural network that is predisposed to follow rules of effective learning and adapts to optimize its chances of long-term success. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model of executive function can facilitate the development of hypothesis testing as an internal reasoning process and might provide insight into observed abilities of human learning and the organization of the human brain.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Whm-2. This is relatively low, as comparisons with models and data from other close approaches showed that the energy flux has significantly decreased as we study the solar wind closer to the solar center. In fact, the average energy flux at a distance of 36.6 times the radius of the solar center, which was found during six other approaches, was about 300 Whm-2, a value somewhat lower than the predicted value from a known model.

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we introduce the concept of a numerable principal bundle with quantum characteristics. A locally trivial G-C*-algebra is considered primitive if it contains a copy of C0(A) for every nontrivial subgroup A of G. We define a G-C*-algebra to be transitively Haar measurable if it possesses a Haar-like measure invariant under the action of every subgroup of G. We establish that strongly transitive, primitive bundles with full action are quantization equivalences, building on a 2006 theorem by E. Størmer. We avenge the counterintuitive results of E. Størmer by showing that for simply connected Lie groups acting uniformly, all transitive bundles with Haar measure are quantization equivalences. We achieve this by proving that the G C*-algebra constructed from a locally compact group with solvable Lie algebra can never be transitive.

We show that any family of maximal almost-disjoint sets can be eliminated via a specific method of adding new elements that preserves the cardinality of $P$-points. Using this finding, we establish that it is possible in a specific set of circumstances that the first uncountable ordinal is less than the least cardinality for uniformization, but the least cardinality for amalgamation is greater, resolving two problems that have been outstanding for nearly 20 years and a further issue proposed by Brendle. Furthermore, we will provide an alternative explanation for why it is consistent that $\mathfrak{u}<\mathfrak{s}$ as proven by Blass and Shelah.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior in a $q$-deformed optomechanical system. This study employs $q$-deformation to model both optical coupling and Brownian interactions between mechanical oscillators, leading to a derivation of $q$-deformed optomechanical equations. Analyzing these equations reveals that $q$-deformation influences phase transitions, including the critical phase transition and soft mode transition. Furthermore, $q$-deformation impacts thermomechanical force, mean field, and fluctuation. This effect arises due to altered fluctuations and absorption/detection processes. Influence of $q$-deformation on second-order quantum effects, including squeezing and entanglement, is also explored. This research provides a theoretical foundation for $q$-deformed optomechanics and suggests possible avenues for $q$-deformation exploration in optomechanical systems.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building upon that work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to accurately predict solution evolution between time steps, circumventing traditional numerical limitations. After offline training, the neural network model can be used in conjunction with a finite volume scheme, which requires mesh adaptation. One distinct advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate CFL restrictions, permitting a wider range of time step sizes. Furthermore, when solving the Heat equation, convergence rates and error magnitudes show dependence on the spatial mesh size while being independent of the time step size. Moreover, the neural network model exhibits exceptional performance in simulating shock waves and rarefaction waves within nonlinear PDEs with enhanced accuracy compared to traditional numerical methods.

The ALICE Collaboration has finalized the upgrade of its detector, with the current phase involving testing to mark the beginning of data collection for LHC Run 3. In conjunction, studies on the experiment's future are underway, with the primary goal being to enhance ALICE's capabilities to analyze high-energy collisions. A proposed enhancement includes the integration of a self-supporting, thin silicon tracker that will be placed inside a new, cryogenic tank containing the present Time-Projection Chamber's detection area. A cutting-edge, global navigation system and advanced readout technology are set to greatly increase the tracker's position resolution and overall efficiency. A crucial aspect of these upgrades will be to refine measurements related to the production of heavy particles and low-mass electron pairs, with potential implications for our understanding of energy scales and the initial conditions of the collisions. In light of this, the present research will serve as a foundation for future LSST, CLAS12, and CBFTC experiments, with the relevant findings set to be presented at relevant international conferences in the coming years.

The Usual Suspects, utilizing Gaussian wave packets, have demonstrated in previous work how the de Sitter decoherence effect produces a quasi-classical vacuum state. In order to study the origin of this quasi-classical vacuum state, we introduce a scalar field in the classical de Sitter space with a time-dependent mass. The Schrödinger-Helmholtz decomposition is then used to separate the flat space part from the quasi-confining part of the scalar field's propagator. Subsequently, various observables are measured within Gaussian windows at late and early times, leading to the discovery of acceleration-dependent Machian redshift and blueshift, which can be reinterpreted as late and early perceptions of a vacuum state, respectively. Importantly, the blueshift at late times is contrary to naive expectations, much like the early perception of a vacuum state. By taking the low-mass limit and combining it with previous work on de Sitter decoherence, we find that our findings not only explain the decoherence effect but also reveal that acceleration contributes to the quasi-classical vacuum state. Moreover, the distinct blueshift and redshift produce a time-reversed picture, which suggests that the de Sitter de Sitter universe could be visually reversed. Lastly, the decomposition of the propagator reveals an interesting structure consisting of a constant, logarithmically increasing and decreasing term. Utilizing Gaussian windows, we are able to isolate these components, which in combination with the low-mass limit

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related entities within a given text. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts to integrate robust entity linking capabilities into existing event extraction systems have been relatively limited. This study addresses this gap by presenting CLIOE, a novel approach that effectively links entities to complex event descriptions, demonstrating its capabilities on the FIBEC dataset through both qualitative and quantitative analysis. Furthermore, CLIOE achieves remarkable performance on the FIBEC dataset, securing first place in both semantic fault-tolerant event extraction and the standard evaluation.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. A crucial aspect of our research involves establishing the validity, pointwise in Chern forms, of the universal push-forward formula for all universal bundles. A fundamental step toward our proof is explicitly determining, at each point of the flag bundle, the Chern curvature of the universal bundles, as endowed with their induced metrics. This leads to the development of an alternative approach to the Jacobi-Trudi identity using differential forms, as well as confirmation of the positivity of specific Chern forms for Griffiths semipositive vector bundles, thus partially supporting Griffiths' conjecture on characteristic forms of positive characteristic.

Observations from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed how a clumpy stellar wind with varying density affects the X-ray binary system Vela X-2, varying its fractional variability power by tenfold. We are modeling this system to investigate how a chaotic wind impacts the accretion disk in high-mass X-ray binaries. Our analysis considers the effects of different wind types and variations in the wind's density, clump size, and distribution. For a typical, radially dependent wind, the accretion disk's variability decreases as the disk's inner radius increases, while increased wind clump size or distribution lowers the system's variability. However, when assuming a chaotic, hydrodynamic wind, the results significantly change. Here, the system's variability significantly increases when the clumps overlap transit times across the outer disk radius and the inner disk edge. For Vela X-2, this corresponds to a particular radius above 50 solar radii. For this high-mass X-ray binary, the system's X-ray spectrum, which is hard X-rays, supports the hydrodynamic wind model. Our findings suggest that hydrodynamic clumps could impact the detection and measurement of high-mass X-ray binary states, which could be misinterpreted as thermal fluctuations.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal states characteristic of high-temperature atherospheres. Where conventional matter particles undergo the Weinberg gravitational selection rule, the non-abelian terms necessitate a revised selection rule, which is investigated in this context.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between excelling at one or the other. To address this issue, researchers are now turning to joint models that simulate human behavior to achieve better results. Our study builds on this trend by developing a new joint model that surpasses individual models in both tasks. To achieve this, we designed a model that integrates a universal decomposition parser and a meaning representation model based on a advanced neural network design. Furthermore, we developed a new metric called ML Loss to optimize performance and applied it to a public dataset. The results show that our model performs better than others in both syntax and semantics parsing, with a notable improvement in semantics loss rate of 9.5% compared to the current best technique.

The formation of magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole following a compact binary merger is a potentially significant event, capable of launching outflows that explain the phenomenon of short gamma ray bursts and kilonovae radiation. By utilizing the detection of gravitational waves from GW170817 by the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) and ground-based optical telescopes, we have established a limit on the mass ejected from the merger, based on optical observations, and have demonstrated that this limit is correlated with the final black hole's rotational speed. Notably, our analysis reveals that less than approximately $5 \times 10^{-5} M_\odot$ of mass is ejected when the final black hole has a rotational speed of 30% of the maximum possible speed, and that this limit decreases exponentially as the rotational speed increases. Therefore, despite previous assumptions, it is highly unlikely that magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole significantly affect the mass loss associated with the detection of GW170817. However, because there is still some amount of mass ejection allowed by the data, it remains possible that magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole could produce a significant amount of mass ejection, leading to the production of gamma rays and the illumination of an accompanying neutron star, thereby resolving long-standing issues related to the energy requirements of gamma ray bursts.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, contained distinct tidal features with flux ratios exceeding one percent. Observations indicated an exponential decline in the number of galaxies as tidal features became more pronounced. Additionally, within our chosen stellar mass range, the frequency of tidal features decreased in comparison to lower mass galaxies. Our statistical findings show that tidal features are primarily found in galaxies undergoing profuse star-forming activities, but are relatively rare among early-type galaxies of similar mass. We found no conclusive evidence to suggest that tidal features significantly impact the mass range of early-type galaxies. Our results will be further utilized to estimate the incidence of tidal interactions within databases that include later-stage tidal debris.

This paper is a component of a research project focusing on the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), a theoretical framework derived from the established equation by Laplace and Poisson. Our study supports the notion that, under specific conditions dependent on the object's spin, the ASTG can generate repulsive gravitational fields in the polar regions of massive objects, a phenomenon similar to the existing observation of the repulsive gravitational behavior in the system consisting of a black hole and a white hole. Furthermore, the analysis conducted within the context of ASTG indicates that its predictions are compatible with the principles of special and general relativity as well as the findings from quantum mechanics, electromagnetism, and thermodynamics.

We have gathered a vast dataset of observations during and around fast radio bursts, which provides the largest observation set of any kind to date. Our research involves analyzing the behavior of flare energies before and after radio bursts, as well as searching for recurring FRBs to constrain the distances of their source locations. Additionally, we examined nearby FRB mills to determine the ages of repeating FRBs and set an upper limit on the distances of non-repeating sources. Our findings support the magnetic dipole model and show significant relationships between repeat counts and gamma-ray flux, spectral indexes, and luminosity in optical transient peaks. These results suggest that a substantial portion of repeating FRBs could be located within 2 Gpc. In contrast, non-repeating FRBs appear to be no more than 400 Mpc away. Our work highlights the importance of future simultaneous observations, especially those that can cover the UV and X-ray bands, to understand the behavior of FRB powers during and after events.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant scientific breakthroughs in various fields, including medicine, defense, and energy, since the 1990s.  Achieving high power from these systems requires accurate analysis of their complex dynamics which involves intricate mathematical modeling.  Due to their intricate nature, these models can be computationally expensive and difficult to comprehend through traditional analysis.  Assisting in understanding the dynamics of these models can be achieved through data-driven methods in two main steps, data training and model assessment.  This paper will discuss the development and application of a specialized neural network, called PHOTONNN, that learns the behavior of photon noise in CPA-NLO systems based on experimental data.  Using reduced order models as a reference, PHOTONNN is trained to predict specific characteristics of these photon distributions.  The study found that PHOTONNN successfully extracts and represents complex information about the nonlinear dynamics in terms of optimized functions and chaos dynamics.  The results showcase that PHOTONNN can determine various features of these photon distributions with high precision even in complex nonlinear scenarios.  The study further indicates that PHOTONNN can identify and distinguish between reduced order models that seem equivalent in terms of forward modeling but have different internal characteristics.  The results also suggest that PHOTONNN can identify areas where these reduced order models fail to accurately predict dynamics in nonlinear systems, that appear stable on the surface but become unstable in the internal state.

Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 can be leveraged for producing high-quality text content, but it is often difficult for untrained models to effectively integrate visual information from images while generating text. This work proposes a new framework called MAGIC that allows a language model to learn an image-based content generator, giving it the ability to condition text generation on multiple visual inputs. By converting an image into a text representation that can be generated by a language model, MAGIC provides a way for the model to learn what types of image content is relevant during text generation. It achieves this through a self-supervised learning task and a guided image-to-text generation process that allows the model to focus on making text predictions based on specific image features. Using a modified version of GPT-2, we were able to improve the model's ability to identify and describe specific image elements, as well as generate more detailed and visually accurate text descriptions, without significantly increasing the model's size or memory requirements.

We introduce an improved RingCT protocol that enables confidential transactions in a decentralized environment. The proposed Delegated RingCT protocol comprises two novel features, Delegation and Minimization, leading to increased computational efficiency and decreased memory requirements. The Delegation feature reduces processing time by incorporating the Sum Hash value early in the decryption process, while Minimization reduces memory usage by limiting the transmission of unnecessary information. The Delegated RingCT protocol enhances the security and privacy of transactions while being compatible with existing RingCT implementations.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address new issues can negatively affect its performance in previously trained tasks. To address this challenge, researchers have developed the 'cooperative continuum learning' framework, based on principles from continuous learning and observations from over 1,000 experiments in mechanical physics. The proposed framework successfully prevents forgetting and allows neural networks to adapt to new situations without losing previously acquired skills. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate that adaptive models can recall established knowledge when reunited with relevant data, demonstrating the potential for a neural network to be transferred from one cooperative project to another. The CSL framework provides an innovative solution, opening doors to complex distributed mechanics modeling and empowering teams to collaborate and develop customized models for specific applications.

Off-shell $K$ matrix amplitudes are used to analyze the decay processes $\Upsilon(10753)$ to $K^+ K^-$, $\Upsilon(10753)$ to $K^0_S K^0_S$, and in combination with vector meson dominance theory, $\Upsilon(10753)$ to $\pi^+ \pi^-$. Results reveal that for the first time, the decay process $\Upsilon(10753)$ to $\pi^+ \pi-$ has a branching ratio greater than $10^{-6}$. Furthermore, the amplitudes are used to produce rate predictions and sensitivity limits for the direct $CP$ difference in $\Upsilon(10753)$ decays into $K^+ K^-$.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a sequence of constrained optimization problems that can be iteratively refined. Our method, AskewSGD, is an efficient first-order stochastic approach that achieves similar generalization performance to conventional gradient descent while offering significant speedup and memory reduction. Our experiments confirm that AskewSGD outperforms existing methods on various real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to train deep learning models with minimal precision.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve robots that more closely resemble the anatomy of invertebrate creatures and flexible body parts of vertebrates. To introduce the concepts and challenges of this innovative area in robotics, we will be adopting a control theorist's approach, simplifying the entry into this field by systematically presenting current research and future obstacles through a controller's viewpoint. We will start with the fundamental principles of continuum robotics, discuss the inherent difficulties of designing controllers for these robots and organize existing work under three key control challenges: maintaining assembly, avoiding obstacles, and recovering from disturbances. We will provide a detailed explanation of each control challenge along with relevant existing work, culminating in a comprehensive analysis of the state of the art in continuum robotics, along with an identification of open problems that are set to pave the way for the advancement of this dynamic field.

Let G^J_1(ℝ) denote the real Jacobi group, which consists of direct products of the special linear group, Heisenberg group, and real numbers. It can be embedded into the real Lie group G^J_2(ℝ), comprising the general linear group GL(3,ℝ), as the latter's natural embedding inherits a natural invariant metric. Similarly, an embedding of the real Jacobi group by GL(2,ℝ) preserves a metric, which in turn induces a naturally metric on the real Jacobi group itself. These embedded metrics exhibit distinct characteristics and may be expressed through distinct parametrizations. We establish a canonical identification of the real Jacobi group to facilitate the comparison and calculation of embedded metrics. We further derive embedded metrics for the real Jacobi group, which takes the form of a Riemannian 6-manifold when treated as a left invariant metric on GL(2,ℝ).

Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, necessitating a model's
understanding of both language and symbolic computations involving data in
tables. Despite pre-trained language models excelling in confirming simple
assertions, they often falter when handling complex assertions requiring
multiple calculations. In addressing this challenge, we introduce a novel
evaluation method for assertion-based fact verification that mirrors real-world
requirements, as well as a pre-trained neural model incorporating both
language modeling and symbolic reasoning capabilities. The proposed model,
structured in a memory-augmented architecture, can accurately calculate
quantitative properties and therefore effectively verifies assertions relying on
data in tables.

The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised approaches, however, current advancements are primarily based on labelled data, leading to increased control, flexibility, and stability in the generated images. Notably, these supervised methods require substantial amounts of annotated data, posing a major challenge. Our proposed framework combines two powerful techniques: adversarial training and representation learning, ultimately enabling the utilisation of limited, weakly labelled image pairs for high-quality image synthesis. Our contribution is notably capable of handling the unsupervised challenge associated with large datasets, like ImageNet, as well as the supervised challenge with smaller datasets, like the WSOP dataset. Our results demonstrate the production of realistic images with notable improvements in every scenario. Our work significantly enables the synthesis of numerous images on an open-source platform, serving as a community-driven reference for the synthesis of synthetic images, as well as a benchmark for the evaluation of generated content. Our repository is hosted at https://github.com/JerryCBerlin/ConditionalGAN.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. Researchers have developed methods like Markov Chain Monte Carlo derivatives for complex, high-dimensional problems. A study examined ten different algorithms, incorporating techniques from slice sampling, hit-and-run, and differential evolution, to determine their efficiency in various 2 to 100 dimensional scenarios, including ellipsoidal, non-ellipsoidal, and non-convex cases. To ensure the results are reliable regardless of the distribution of the posteriors, the nested sampling shrinkage test was used to evaluate mixing capabilities. Compared to slice sampling, algorithms like hit-and-run and whitened hit-and-run demonstrated improved performance under similar step limits, with small dimensional losses in whitenedness for the latter. Additionally, incorporating WhiNED in the NIMING method enhanced scalability compared to shotgun sampling, decreasing time and number of candidate generations while increasing efficiency by up to 20 times.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any three points' labels allows us to deduce the direct distance between any two of them, excluding the third. Our work proves that any weighted network with a specific layout (or in fact any network with a limited number of non-linear elements) has a brief description system where at most $2n - 3$ labels are required, and this limit is optimal. Notably, this is the first general proof that such a system exists in networks with basic properties, and it significantly improves the existing ones by removing a factor of at least two. However, our work shows that some properties of the network structure are needed to ensure the existence of such a system, as it's easily seen that single-cycle networks do not meet this criterion.

In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a fermionic system with a locally interacting bare spectrum, specifically a simple tight-binding model with nearest-neighbor interactions on a one-dimensional lattice. Correlation functions are calculated directly in the Schrödinger picture by considering the time derivative of a product of two fermionic fields, expressed as a wave function that belongs to a finite-dimensional Liouvillian space. This Liouvillian wave function is constructed by solving a generalized eigenvalue problem, and its imaginary part at the Liouvillian frequency, specifically at the point of a pole, is shown to be a measure of oscillation frequency. Furthermore, we determine the scaling behavior of this frequency with system size by employing the matrix product state method, specifically the density-matrix renormalization group, in the real-time formalism. We find that the frequency scales subdiffusively with system size, consistent with previous studies on static correlations, and we attribute this behavior to the emergence of a localization phase in the real-time evolution of the many-body system.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\lambda$, defined within a bounded $\mathbb{R}^2$ domain $\Omega$ and satisfying specific smoothness and boundedness conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the weak solution in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ for the Dirichlet problem, where $2<p<\infty$, assuming that the equation also includes source and flux terms. Similar results are obtained for the corresponding dual problem under analogous conditions.

To ensure that medical imaging models produce accurate predictions, it is crucial to implement out-of-distribution detection capabilities. There are doubts whether traditional deep neural network-based methods are effective in identifying shifts in medical imaging domains. In contrast, Gaussian Processes offer a more robust method for statistical inference and out-of-distribution detection. However, the computational efficiency of Gaussian Processes needs to be improved to make them practical for use in deep learning models. This study proposes a Stochastic Variational Sparse Gaussian Process regression method that aims to improve the efficiency of Gaussian Process regression by leveraging inferences from smaller GP models. This approach claims to be up to 25 times more efficient than traditional Bayesian methods, while also accelerating runtime by up to 100 times. The method's performance was tested on changes in digital pathology images and found to be more accurate than other detectors, including a popular UNet-based alternative.

Quantum systems driven periodically experience decay due to internal losses and interactions with surroundings.  In most cases, a system in contact with heat will eventually reach balance.  However, when driven and coupled to a heat bath, system behavior can become more complex, displaying periodic decay and later a prolonged period of stable existence, known as an Arnold tongue.  Although generally found in systems of thermodynamic importance, thermodynamic quantities in such systems are difficult to measure.  A challenge arises in experimental analysis, as this phenomenon appears as part of a broader phase diagram and requires precise differentiation from surrounding phases.  A proposed approach involves measuring relaxation times after a sudden change in conditions to distinguish Arnold tongues from nearby phases.  Future experiments should take this approach to identify the locations of Arnold tongues and understand how they impact system evolution.  Interestingly, a comparison of theoretical and theoretical models shows an unanticipated high level of agreement between them, implying that commonly used models of driven quantum systems accurately represent the results of actual quantum simulations.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ of the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in an open convex domain with a nonnegative, bounded right-hand side, along with specific boundary data. A key finding relates Alexandrov's maximum principle, specifically its equivalence to H\"older continuity, for convex functions with zero boundary data. Furthermore, it has been proven that convex $\alpha$-H\"older continuous functions fall into $W^{1,p}$ for $p<1/(1{-}\alpha)$. Crucially, this research establishes the H\"older continuity of the convex solution $u$ under specific boundary data, with sharp bounds for the exponent derived through a method involving a bounding Hessian determinant on an n-dimensional cylinder.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable oscillators was a complex task that often resulted in cumbersome devices. Thanks to advancements in technology, precise timekeeping is now achievable with simple, non-linear systems, including mechanical and biological ones. Although biological systems operate outside the realm of classical mechanics, their periodic behavior is a testament to their utility in timekeeping. We propose a design framework that transforms a chaotic system into a reliable clock, operating within a fundamental limit. Eliminating randomness in clicking mechanisms and rectifying time discrepancies allows us to substitute conventional periodic systems with ones generating random events. This adaptation retains the inherent stability of the original system, making it suitable for timekeeping applications. As an illustration, we modified a universally accessible model based on the work by T. Yalcin for achieving timekeeping capabilities.

This research centers on Software Defined Networks (SDN) to address the challenges of traffic engineering, fault prevention, and service delivery within reliability and energy constraints. Utilizing Fog computing, we focus on optimizing distributed traffic flows to achieve real-time service delivery, effective failure recovery, and fault-awareness in the context of Service Function Chains (SFCs). To address these issues, we present an energy and delay constrained traffic routing problem at the network layer, and a novel optimization algorithm for fault-conscious SFC delivery in the context of energy constraints. Our first-congested path algorithm based on the Hurwitz zeta function, HZFirstConcPath, outperforms existing approaches by minimizing energy consumption while delivering more service through multiple SFCs. Simulation results demonstrate that our models produce minimal energy consumption while delivering services at an increased rate of 2.13, 1.85, and 1.78 times over other conventional methods.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss term is crucial for image retrieval. Various
proposals have been made to enhance its effectiveness, however there's been little
exploration into the internal workings of pair-wise loss constructions. This gap
in knowledge makes it difficult to fully comprehend how to ramp down pair-wise
loss and how to adjust its scale. This paper hopes to bridge this gap by introducing
a comprehensive framework that involves evaluating and comparing the internal
structure of pair-wise losses, ultimately leading to the development of large
-scale image retrieval tasks.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as templates for creating codes capable of correcting quantum errors, and embody dynamics influenced by dynamic optimization processes. A key feature of these networks is their ability to be effectively translated into Euclidean space geometries. We outline a generic framework for constructing networks based on the process of optimisation, and provide specific instances of these networks - comprised of gluing optimised two-dimensional shapes together. We thoroughly examine a particular instance of this class, known as half-space networks, and demonstrate their capacity for simulating space-time dynamics, as well as their connection to Euclidean regions corresponding to three-dimensional volumes. Furthermore, we discuss the network's property of local consistency and its precise physical significance, and show that this property can be extended to include diverse physical scenarios. Additionally, we derive a set of practical practical practical rules that govern how quantum operators interact within the network, and illustrate this principle using the case of a scalar field.

Our study of magnetized radio filaments at the center of the galaxy reveals clustered groups that resemble comb patterns with multiple teeth, as well as loop-like features that could be indicative of composite filament formations. A relatively high-frequency radio map shows grouped filaments aligned in an east-west direction and spaced approximately 10 parsecs apart. Close examination of these groups and their distances yields several key findings: group sizes correlate with spacing, and each group has a distinct size-range; there's a distinct 'U'-shaped relationship between group size and distance. Two potential explanations exist for these observations: grouped filaments might be formed from combs of magnetic field structures either perpendicular to a plate-like galaxy floor or pressed against it. In the former scenario, filament grouping would reflect magnetic field cell size adjusted for line-of-sight depth, and in the latter, adjusted for both depth and pressure from a galactic floor. Observations of filaments shifting in response to motion and changes in density support the latter theory, suggesting that galaxy compression played a role in filament formation, bringing magnetized plasma to the center and causing it to twist, reflecting a predominantly right-handed spiral structure. Magnetized plasma level in the center might be low, causing it to appear that filament grouping is mostly along the north-south axis rather than the true east-west alignment due to limited, variable 3D depth perception.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems by optimizing DERs through the scheduling of smart inverters. The method considers primary-secondary networks and loads influenced by voltage. The system complexity is minimized through the creation of zones in the network based on connectivity. To address non-linearities from load models and power flow, the paper suggests a linear approximation technique using power and voltage measurements, enabling the online implementation of the proposed control for tracking fast system variations led by DERs. The method also allows for non-uniform update rates and robust communication in the presence of delays and failures. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through numerical testing on a real U.S. Midwest distribution feeder.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where the user obtains extended, unified feedback records, encompassing past, present, and future choices and rewards, potentially with look-ahead capabilities, enabling them to select actions before receiving rewards. While delayed settings have been extensively studied in the experts' scenario, where rewards are determined by a teacher, this problem is relatively unexplored in the bandits' case. Notably, any method for delayed bandits will simultaneously solve the problem for delayed experts by determining the teacher's optimal action using the developed strategies. In response, we devise a new algorithm that simultaneously achieves the best possible outcome in both delayed bandits and experts. Notably, this algorithm is the first to directly solve delayed bandits with a minimal additional loss, as opposed to previous methods. Notably, this algorithm's flexibility is highlighted by its ability to solve non-stochastic bandits with a minimal additional loss, as well as its ability to solve delayed experts with a minimal additional loss, comparable to the best existing algorithms. Furthermore, this algorithm's outcome is closely linked to a new lower bound, marking the first for delayed bandits, thereby illustrating the inherent drawbacks of delayed settings in terms of regret in comparison to immediate feedback.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed. Specifically, optimizing task success may come at the cost of lexical diversity, and relying on existing datasets can perpetuate and even intensify this issue. To better understand and address this problem, we investigated how reinforcement learning impacts the predictability of words in task-oriented dialogue tasks. Our study found that RL methods that reward task success lead to a less predictable vocabulary. To combat this effect, we developed and tested an alternative reinforcement learning approach that incorporates neural language models. This new method, called the Policy Network Generator, improves results by maintaining higher lexical diversity without compromising task performance.

Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened doors for in-depth numerical analyses of QCD's non-perturbative features, exemplified in the initial studies by Michael Creutz. Subsequently, investigations into the QCD phase diagram and the thermodynamics of hot, dense strong-interaction matter gained significant momentum. In this concise review, some key outcomes from over four decades of lattice QCD research on QCD thermodynamics are compiled.

A type of Gaussian process regression that accounts for the variability in data points, called heteroscedastic Gaussian process regression, is often used for modeling load responses on offshore wind turbines. However, this approach has some limitations as it assumes the uncertainties in the data follow a specific pattern, which may not always be the case in real-world situations. In response to this limitation, a new method, called nonparametric heteroscedastic Gaussian process regression, has been proposed, that removes this assumption and instead directly estimates the noise parameters in the data. In practical applications, this method can be computed efficiently by combining smaller calculations, making it suitable for use in predictive maintenance. In simulations, the new method demonstrated better accuracy than other similar approaches, and when used to analyze data from a specific offshore wind turbine, it was able to accurately forecast the turbine's structural responses and predict its remaining useful life.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining and natural language processing techniques, we examine public sentiment towards the Turkish Earthquake Institute (EMKO), local authorities, and the government following the incident. Our results reveal significant drops in public trust in these institutions, with real-time sentiment analysis and sentiment switching detection enabling us to grasp complex public emotions.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms of Z[G] induce trivial permutations when applied to the twisted conjugacy classes. The class $R_\infty$ is a specific instance of more extensive sets of groups, particularly those exhibiting property $FC$. The class $R_\infty$ encompasses all solvable groups, particularly finitely generated ones. The objective of this research paper is to demonstrate two key findings related to $R_\infty$ classes of groups. Firstly, we will prove via direct demonstration that arrest of growth, a phenomenon characteristic of some linear groups, is a direct consequence of a group exhibiting $R_\infty$. Furthermore, we will derive additional implications of this phenomenon, highlighting how it impacts other distinct properties unique to $R_\infty$ classes of groups.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. Our solution relies on a fitting method with a multi-stage, nested structure that isolates variables at multiple levels of detail, allowing us to directly analyze the overall reaction pathway as well as the immediate surroundings of the initial and final states. By comparing our results with existing studies using a different technique, we find that the new approach leads to consistent findings. Furthermore, applying our technique to examine transfer processes between different types of excitations, we identify key steps in the reaction mechanism that can be observed with other techniques. Lastly, we demonstrate that our technique is stable against continuous changes in the reaction mechanism and can accurately determine fine details of the reaction process, even when incorporating additional constraints.

This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented vehicle data collected in downtown Indianapolis over the course
of 68 driving sessions with various drivers. Each session lasted approximately
20 to 40 minutes. Our primary aim in creating this dataset is to supply the
research community with realistic driving scenarios encompassing diverse
trajectories and driving behaviors. SceNDD features a comprehensive set of data,
including the ego-vehicle's waypoints, velocity, and yaw angle, as well as
similar metrics for non-ego actors. Additionally, we allow users to customize
existing scenarios by introducing additional elements, such as actors, sensors,
lanes, roads, and obstacles. A Joint Probabilistic Data Association tracker was
utilized to identify non-ego vehicles. We present some preliminary outcomes of
the dataset, along with potential applications, and anticipate the complete
release of SceNDD in early 2023.

In connection with the information paradox problem, theories such as BCFT and ICFT are gaining attention. As a contribution to this area of study, we have developed an approach to reflected entropy in the context of BCFT/ICFT. Starting with BCFT as our framework, we defined reflected entropy through a specific procedure, then showed its stronger monotonic property. Additionally, we proposed a formula for the reflected entropy of a boundary interval in BCFT, where we considered the dual ICFT to interpret the results. According to our proposal, the reflected entropy is proportional to the area of the cross section of the entangement wedge, which is an general aspect of holographic theories. We have verified the proposal using numerical data from several theories with different features. We have also extended our proposal to the context of 2D massive field theories.

Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has intensified in the field of wireless communication due to their potential for controlling the propagation environment and minimizing interference effectively. However, the accuracy of channel estimation in such systems can be compromised by the high time-domain auto-correlation of cisoidal signals, which causes large estimation error and impedes the development of reliable algorithms. In this study, a new channel estimation method was successfully developed to extract the frequency-domain reflections in cisoidal signals, which were previously obscured by heavy auto-correlation. By extracting these signals, the estimated error is significantly reduced, thereby paving the way for the development of reliable ris-assisted OFDM systems. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method surpasses existing approaches, thereby providing solid groundwork for the design and implementation of ris-assisted OFDM systems.

We are investigating a type of equality related to the work exerted on a system, which involves comparing energy measurements to calculate a work exerted by a quantum source. We establish the minimum requirements for certain system properties, including how precisely energy is measured and its available thermal states, in order to achieve maximum efficiency. In the context of the Otto cycle, we demonstrate that these conditions allow us to replicate a crucial step using a thermalized qubit as a quantum source. We also examine the degradation of this process and compare it to other optimal protocols previously proposed.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on minimally connected 7-dimensional homogeneous spaces with G2 structure.

The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and socio-economic disruption, with contact tracing being a critical component of the efforts to contain the outbreak. Although digital contact tracing methods have been widely adopted, they pose significant concerns regarding data security, including potential invasion of individuals' privacy and the risk of discriminatory actions. To mitigate these issues, we propose an secure contact tracing system that combines contact detection with privacy protection. The proposed system consists of two modules: Contact Tracing Module and Diagnostics Module. The Contact Tracing Module handles contact detection, while the Diagnostics Module handles COVID-19 diagnosis. A detailed explanation of the proposed system's operating process can be found in Section 5.3.

The central nervous system's underlying physiological processes that drive conscious experiences have long been the focal point of research in cognitive neuroscience. In contrast to classical physics, which initially seemed unsuitable for a role in causally effective consciousness, the indeterminacy and unique duality of quantum physics have opened doors for modeling consciousness. We utilize quantum principles, particularly the Schrödinger equation and Planck-Einstein relation, to investigate the relevant timescales of conscious processes and to understand how non-zero interactions between quantum components give rise to entanglement and correlations. We demonstrate, employing a measure of entanglement based on Schmidt decomposition, that interactions between quantum subsystems can generate both entanglement and decoherence, which in turn enable dynamic changes in the entanglement of composite states. In contrast, coherence of individual subsystems is insufficient for binding, whereas interactions and associated decoherence play a crucial role in shaping quantum entanglement and correlations.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A cluster of young compact asteroids connected to 39991 Iochroma undergoes a dynamics analysis in this study. Our findings show the Iochroma family's location within two adjacent three-body resonance zones - specifically 3J-1M-3 and 5J 3S-2. This paper establishes the precise positioning of these resonances as well as their demarcation boundary, providing orbital elements approximations that can inform future Iochroma family dynamics research. Moreover, the study identifies a previously unrecognized member of this family, asteroid 2016 UT3.

Building upon Ramanujan's well-known formula for odd zeta values, we establish a related expression using the Hurwitz zeta function. We introduce a novel integral kernel that relates to the Hurwitz zeta function and serves as an extension of the integral kernel linked to Ramanujan's identity. Additionally, we deduce various infinite families of identities comparable to Ramanujan's formula.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Recent uses of machine learning in algebraic geometry and physics are explored,  
revealing how problems in this field can be easily translated into tensor mapping,  
a concept suitable for supervised learning, as well as offering a chance to use unsupervised  
methods to analyze geometrical data. A primary aspect of this project involves understanding  
how to use geometry within machine learning, as well as how artificial intelligence can be applied
