We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight factors and α > 1. This outcome addresses an unresolved issue in reference \cite{JANSON}, with the added consideration of cases where q is greater than or equal to 2, while providing related estimates for 0 < q < 2.

Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which
takes several days and sometimes produces incorrect results. Computed Tomography
scans can provide valuable assistance with COVID-19 diagnosis, although they expose
patients to a significant amount of radiation, which can be detrimental to those
requiring multiple scans. To address this issue, we studied low-dose and ultra-low
dose scan protocols, which minimize radiation levels while maintaining image
quality suitable for diagnostic purposes. Since qualified experts might be scarce
during a pandemic, we designed an artificial intelligence framework using a dataset
of low-dose and ultra-low dose scans, testing its ability to match the performance
of medical professionals. The model, based on a two-stage capsule network
architecture, successfully avoided overfitting and demonstrated its effectiveness
by achieving an accuracy of 94.5% for pulmonary lesions, which is comparable to
the performance of human radiologists (95% and 96.7% for normal and lung abnormal
images respectively). The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com
/PracticalIntelligence/LowDoseCovidNet.

As numerous satellite constellations in the low-Earth orbit region are scheduled to be deployed, the rate at which they occupy space needs to be quantified to assess the level of operational overlap. To do this, the term space occupancy will be used to describe the fraction of low-Earth orbit space occupied by a given satellite population, defined as the proportion of satellites within a specific altitude range that have overlapped with another satellite within the same range and same time period. This concept builds on the definition of channel occupancy from the field of channel assignment. An analytical model has been developed to calculate both short-term and long-term space occupancy in a homogeneous population, assuming uniform orbital elevations and equal birth rates among the satellites. Furthermore, the model has been adapted to account for the phenomenon of death beds, where deceased satellites immediately release their space. It is anticipated that the knowledge of low-Earth orbit satellite distributions will be necessary to determine space occupancy, highlighting the significance of this parameter in evaluating and comparing different satellite constellations.

To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous irregular points is initially created, which allows for intricate quad configurations due to its unstructured layout. Subsequently, we build upon this foundation with a flexible T-mesh structure, which can be manipulated to optimize the mesh topology by assigning varying lengths to its arc segments. Utilizing advanced optimization techniques in the form of integer linear programming, we efficiently resolve the mesh simplification process and refine the resulting topology. Ultimately, we extract high-order quadrilateral meshes from the optimized framework, showcasing excellent results on various CAD models through rigorous testing that highlights their accuracy, visual and quality characteristics, and computational efficiency.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association between variables. The strength of this association can be interpreted using a specific scale, which users can then decide whether the relationship is significant or not by conducting a test. The reliability of this test largely depends on data's normality and the presence of a linear relationship between variables. The purpose of this paper is to introduce a novel test for correlation that is robust against certain forms of data contamination. This new test is also adaptable to non-normal datasets and variables with different distributions. The proposed test is compared with existing methods through simulation studies using real-life data that contains outliers for further validation.

We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix framework for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. Our focus lies in proving that mild solutions derived from the Navier-Stokes equations remain consistently bounded over time when considered within specific function spaces. Initially, we establish the existence of bounded solutions within the Lebesgue spaces and subsequently, we demonstrate the existence of bounded solutions within more critical Hölder spaces. Our study builds upon prior findings by many others and provides further insight into the well-posedness of the Navier-Stokes equations. Our results serve as improvements to prior work and help to address long-standing questions within the field.

Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across specific contexts. A potential solution 
is introduced in this study: the LitMind Dictionary, an online dictionary platform 
accessible through a web interface. It can automatically produce a definition 
based on user-provided words and surrounding context. Furthermore, the LitMind 
Dictionary supports multilingual queries, enabling the generation of definitions 
for Chinese and English, as well as cross-language inquiries between these two 
languages. A simplified user interface enables quick comprehension of query terms 
and enhances the overall user experience. The LitMind Dictionary is open-source, 
and the code, as well as data used in its development, are openly available on 
GitHub.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a classical post-hoc model utilizing surrogates demonstrates dependence on the model itself, thus a reliable post-hoc model for complex models like neural networks is still under research.

Quantum devices based on superconducting properties may be effectively produced
using semiconductor-superconductor hybrids, consisting of materials in close
contact and a well-formed connection. The surface energy levels of materials like
InAs, characterized by a narrow band gap, are specifically positioned close to
their conduction bands. This work focuses on near-surface InAs quantum wells and
their structural characteristics. The surface texture and temperature of the
growth process of the support layer directly affect electron movement. The use of
a capping layer composed of In$_{0.81}$Al$_{0.19}$As demonstrates its capacity
to adjust the positioning of the surface energy levels of the first nanometer of
this thin layer. The electron density measured experimentally is consistent with
predictions from the Schr\"odinger-Poisson calculations, suggesting that the
surface energy levels of the In$_{0.81}$Ga$_{0.19}$As and In$_{0.81}$Al$_{0.19}$
As layers are \SI{40}{\milli eV} and \SI{309}{\milli eV} above the Fermi level
respectively.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization (ERM), a robust measure of model accuracy. Our first learning model utilizes local membership queries (LMQs), where the learner can verify the labels of nearby points to the training sample. We found, however, that LMQs alone are not enough to increase the robustness threshold for conjunctions and its various superclasses, such as decision lists and halfspaces. To address this issue, we developed a new type of query, matestification queries (MQ), which asks if a condition is satisfied for a set of close points. We created a new algorithm for utilizing MQs that is able to learn any class determined by a monotone ANR set family (a class of sets) on the surface of a unit hypercube using an empirical robust minimization (ERM) model. This new algorithm is the first to utilize robustness threshold for conjunctions and its various superclasses, or close spaces (halfspaces, decision lists), and our experiment shows its effectiveness for two real-world datasets.

Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two key concepts, Lower-ColLinear Triangular Matrices and Upper-ColLinear Triangular Matrices. By showing that multiplying these matrices with vectors can be achieved in $O(N)$ operations and demonstrating their closure under specific operations like Hadamard product and matrix scaling, we resolved two critical challenges for IPOT complexity reduction. This breakthrough allows us to minimize the number of iterations, yielding the Fast Sinkhorn II algorithm, a method for computing optimal transport with complexity as low as $O(N)$, even when dealing with large scaling factors and negative costs. Comprehensive numerical tests stress the new algorithm's robustness and efficiency, showcasing its capabilities with various systems.

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planets inside its debris disk, presents an extraordinary chance to study these impacts in relation to age and orbital distance. Our study entails over five hours of Hubble Space Telescope observations of AU Mic's Far-UV spectrum and catalogs 12 newly discovered emission lines, identifying their energies and proposing possible formations for 11 of these lines and 1 previously detected one. Our model simulations suggest that specific atmospheric components may be created or destroyed as a result of the photochemistry caused by the star's high energy radiation. We also discover that some energy levels within the observed X-ray spectrum cannot be explained by the star's older coronal age, necessitating the presence of younger ($\sim$1 Myr) Fe-rich plasma possibly associated with stellar flares. Our models indicate that these events may eject material from AU Mic b's atmosphere, potentially making the planet unhabitable, while current atmospheric water levels appear insufficient for supporting surface liquid water.

We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a homogeneous medium. We introduce a novel effective theory, incorporating a complex term in the magnetic field derivative to replicate non-dissipative friction from radiation. A model based on a Lagrangian framework is formulated, which naturally leads to the identification of an 'effective radius' to quantify radiation loss. We calculate the work done by the system in relation to this energy loss, confirming it matches the outcome obtained directly from the Landau-Lifshitz-Gell-Mann-Eilenberger equation. Furthermore, we extend our model to an anisotropic crystal by adding a Berry phase term to the Lagrangian, which results in the identification of 'effective gaps' to quantify spin-orbit and orbital contributions to radiation loss.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets where the majority classes outweigh minority ones. Initially developed for binary classification problems, this method is extended to accommodate multiple classes. Unlike existing over-sampling techniques that involve generating fake data points, this method achieves replicable results by sidestepping pseudo observation generation. Moreover, this method has demonstrated Bayesian risk consistency when applied to multi-class datasets, whereas previously, such consistency was largely theoretical and applicable only to binary datasets.

We employ photometry data from multiple sources to identify ultra-bright Quasi-Stellar Objects (QSOs) located at distant regions of space. By utilizing SkyMapper's DR3, along with 2MASS, VHS, and other datasets, we successfully isolate nearly 170 QSOs positioned at high redshifts. Our research examines the brightness distribution of SkyMapper's QSO sample at multiple wavelengths to determine the QSO luminosity function. By normalizing this function with a standard formula, we calculate the number density of QSOs per unit volume at redshifts between 3 and 4 as $D_{X(3,4)} = (2.8 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-5}$ mag$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-3}$ for a wavelength of 5500 Å. For QSOs at redshifts between 4.2 and 5.4, we determine the number density as $D_{X(4.2,5.4)} = (5.2 \pm 0.4) \times 10^{-6}$ mag$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-3}$ for the same wavelength. These findings align with predictions from mathematical models, supporting their accuracy. Furthermore, we estimate QSO lifetime and merit the need for QSO surveys that cover a broader wavelength range and span a longer time period.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible information. Our research has also given us insight into a type of quantum coherence known as entanglement, specifically between the quantum dot and the superconducting island. Our findings open the door for future research focused on the interaction between spin and charge transport in superconducting circuits, which could lead to the development of quantum computers based on Majorana modes and new types of entangled systems.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. To expand upon existing work, we introduce a new metric that can accommodate spatial variations and use it to establish conditions under which shockwaves in a broader class of systems, such as fluid flow equations, will behave predictably. Furthermore, we identify specific criteria that certain types of shockwaves must meet in order to be expected to behave predictably. Our investigation into these conditions includes the study of two-fluid dynamics models with and without magnetic forces, as well as fluid flow equations, for which we analyze the interaction between different types of shockwaves under various scenarios without assuming small initial disturbances.

We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel long-distance views by learning to simulate camera movements and image transformations. Our results demonstrate that conditioned diffusion models excel at extending long scenes while accurately maintaining both overall and fine details, surpassing previous methods based on GANs.

Many complex systems exhibit multifaceted characteristics such as coexistence of order and randomness, diversity in patterns and scenarios, and multiple underlying processes. In this paper, we demonstrate a universal approach to uncovering these complex dynamics through a simple method inspired by random walks, which allows us to identify hidden nonlinear relationships in networks with random structures. Our method involves creating a probability equation based on a given network and then using it to measure the nonlinear properties of network nodes. Our theoretical analysis shows that these nonlinear properties can be used to estimate a network's topological features, and this idea has been applied to a variety of complex systems, including mammalian networks and networks of biological cells, with successful results. Furthermore, our method has also led to new insights into how random nonlinear systems change in response to internal or external factors and how they evolve over time.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on the instability of a liquid film. This model demonstrates that slip reduces the rate at which perturbations grow, but surprisingly, it also decreases the rate at which these perturbations reach a critical size that leads to collapse. Contrary to what happens with spherical bubbles, reducing slip actually increases the maximum radius that perturbations can achieve before collapsing. This theoretical understanding is reinforced by a comparison with simulations.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two human evaluators measured and compared the coronal image deformity angles acquired from both robotic and manual scans. The results showed that robotic scanning yielded highly reliable results both within and between evaluators, with minimal difference compared to the manual approach in terms of coronal deformity angles. Furthermore, robotic scanning exhibited accurate intra-rater consistency, with the mean absolute deviation within an acceptable range for the vast majority of measurements. This study found that robotic scanning yields scoliosis deformity angles comparable to those obtained through manual scanning using three-dimensional imaging techniques.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of sentences.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the achievements of 12 models, combining their outputs to evaluate their overall performance in both tasks. Although models excelled in task one, their results were inconsistent in task two. We explored the potential of combining individual models as a means to enhance results and discovered that such collaboration often yielded improved performance in task two but rarely improved task one.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in how they allow subnetworks to learn and share features. In response, we introduce an innovative 'unmixing' procedure for MIMO networks to facilitate shared feature learning among subnetworks. Our preliminary results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, yielding feature sharing and better performance in smaller network configurations.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents through image-based techniques. Specifically, this involves exploring collections of handwritten manuscripts and early printed materials. Acquiring suitable datasets for research on historical documents employing various machine learning methodologies necessitates identifying appropriate datasets. Unfortunately, selecting datasets from the diverse pool of data, varying in script, format, degradation level, label representation, evaluation processes, and benchmarks poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, this research conducts a meta-analysis on available document image datasets. A thorough search through academic databases along with manual collection of datasets from renowned organizations yielded a substantial number of datasets, however, this study could not meet the demand for updated datasets, newly introduced datasets regularly being released. Through this meta-analysis, the authors identified several prominent datasets, categorized these into handwritten and printed material groups, discussed their utilities, outlined their demographics, evaluated data quality, and demonstrated the application of state-of-the-art algorithms on these datasets. Furthermore, the authors highlighted existing gaps in available datasets along with areas of improvement and prospective research directions.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in transmission systems, which causes waviness in robot wrists, leading to suboptimal performance in tasks that necessitate high precision. For these robots, the solution often lies in pairing them with an additional layer of precision-enhancing technology, which comes with added expenses. An innovative approach has been devised to upgrade such machines by tackling the source of the problem itself, involving the implementation of an algorithmic solution to eliminate positional error associated with backlash.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. This perspective considers early life experiences and later behavioral choices as interacting and influencing future health outcomes. In contrast, our proposed model expands on the socioeconomic theory of human capital and incorporates the concept of human health capital. By acknowledging the long-term impact of early life circumstances on future health, this model provides insights into how investments in health can affect future earning potential. In turn, increased earning capacity enables greater financial investment in health, though declining health may also impede an individual's economic progress. We validate these hypotheses using British Whitehall data, analyzing how early life conditions, as embodied by cognitive ability and educational attainment, influence future health, which in turn affects an individual's career advancement and future earning potential. Furthermore, our approach tackles several challenges associated with estimating dynamic models, including the correlation between error terms, potential reverse causality issues, and the problem of unobserved confounding variables. To address these challenges, we employ a Bayesian method, specifically a nonparametric specification for the utility function and the Markov process used to model health changes. Our results demonstrate that a dynamic model, which takes into account changing health, can provide significant insights into the most effective strategies for improving health outcomes.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly as distance increases. This method relies on a set of carefully chosen Gaussian functions to break down integrals into manageable parts. Although the initial implementation assumed uniform distribution of functions, a new, improved method places additional weight on points closest to the atomic nuclei. This modification ensures that all functions associated with a given atomic site have been accounted for, eliminating the need to apply an additional correction term. Notably, the strategy does not necessitate a thorough examination of the entire integration domain, saving significant time and computational resources. A comprehensive collection of highly optimized, open-source tools for evaluating various types of electronic integrals in complex molecular systems is also provided.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by the vertex cover number yielding fixed-parameter tractability. However, the complexity under different parameters remained unclear until our recent discovery, where the problem was found to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the feedback vertex set number. Additionally, we found that parameterization by the vertex cover number results in the problem not admitting a polynomial kernel unless a significant assumption holds. While the problem remains open under the vertex cover number, we found fixed-parameter tractability when parameterizing the problem by distance to cluster or co-cluster.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with multi-million year histories, yet the internal dynamics of these environments are poorly understood. A lack of data has made it difficult to study hothouse climates. A new hothouse climate model, driven by energy balance dynamics, is developed in this study to fill this knowledge gap. The model's stability and stability stability analysis reveal that it shares characteristics with systems that have multi-scale cycling behavior. Long-term simulations show that this type of climate is prone to internal shifts in its atmospheric circulation patterns. As a result of this shift, there is a change in the water cycle, with more extreme variations in its different stages. Compared to a stable climate, the hothouse climate has a greater difference in its water release and absorption processes. In response to a hypothetical 'hothouse on a on a slab' model, our simulations showed that there is a great difference in the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, with more water vapor in the hothouse climate. However, this difference is less pronounced in the actual hothouse climate, with less water vapor in the atmosphere. This study provides new evidence of the internal working of hothouse climates, with more water vapor in the atmosphere, but less in total.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within a broader class of theories proposed by Distler and Gross, while its higher-spin counterparts are part of a larger family of theories explored in related studies. Despite the complexity, an explicit solution exists for the spin-off variant in a simple scenario with one dimension. This find ties in with theories suggesting that twistor actions provide the most suitable description of the fundamental magnetic flux states observed in some quantum systems.

In the application of medical image classification, the quality of the training set is often compromised by the introduction of noise during the annotation process, which stems from the subjective labeling criteria used. To mitigate the adverse effects of noise, research has focused on identifying efficient strategies for removing it to improve the overall performance of the model. Specifically, one research thread explores utilizing the characteristics of the images themselves to create a cleaning filter, which can be adapted to different types of noise. This study contributes to this research thread by proposing a universal filter capable of correcting various common errors in medical image classification datasets, which can be easily integrated into existing classification frameworks with marginal computational costs. Moreover, our work reveals the potential of combining image enhancement and classification tasks into a single stage via transfer learning, which can yield significant improvements in classification accuracy. Through our analysis of several public datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed filter can restore the accuracy of misclassified images in both training and testing stages, thereby enhancing the performance of existing models without requiring further training.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the number of nodes $c$.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and an explicit formula is given for the characteristic polynomial of the CRW's transition probability matrix, utilising a determinant expression related to the graph's generalized weighted zeta function. This is exemplified in the cases of regular graphs and semiregular bipartite graphs. Additionally, the CRW is considered in a different graph scenario.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present three new clock mechanisms that integrate seamlessly with HOL's function logic, making it easier to define terminating functions. By comparing these solutions to a similar approach developed in Isabelle/HOL, we examine how each clock mechanism facilitates the simplification of commonly occurring patterns in program correctness proofs.

The accuracy of models predicting the spatial arrangement of instantaneously occurring wall-bound flows is heavily reliant on the geometric characteristics of the representative structures they employ. This study aims to establish a new approach for identifying the 3-D geometric characteristics of significant, swirling wall currents present in such flows. Furthermore, it is proposed that a similar method can be applied to predict the spatial variation of wall friction associated with these structures. To achieve this, this study compares the geometric characteristics of 3-D spiral vortex representations against direct numerical simulation data of the turbulent/natural separation zone found in the zero-pressure gradient boundary layer at the rear of the Honda Road Car. Ultimately, this study seeks to establish a statistical relationship between the geometric characteristics of these structures and their influence on Reynolds stress, thereby allowing for the prediction of changes in wall friction through a data-driven approach. Current research has only reached a point where it is possible to make a preliminary correlation for the most dominant structures within the simulation dataset.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field behavior. The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an energy lower bound, with corresponding self-dual equations whose solutions manifest as the limiting solitons that achieve this bound. The lower bound on energy, known as the Bogomol'nyi bound, exhibits proportionality to the topological charge of the Skyrme current, thereby being quantized. Conversely, the total energy is bound from above by a Bogomol'nyi bound related to a magnetic part of the baby Skyrme model, thereby quantized as well.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has an orbital magnetic flux of $p/q$ with $0\le p \le q-1$, we studied its phase structure under minimal coupling to a scalar potential in the $q=3$ case. Our analysis revealed that for $0\le p \le 2$, the phase is a Weyl semimetal with a time-reversal-breaking unit of measure $\tau=p mod q$. Specifically, it contains one Weyl node at the k point in the Brillouin torus with momentum $m_n/m_q$. Our calculations showed that as the scalar potential grows from zero, a topological transition occurs, transforming the semimetal phase into a chiral liquid with a nonquantized orbital magnetization. Our findings were verified through numerical investigations, confirming that the results are resilient against variations in the orbital magnetic field intensity and the precise form of the scalar potential. In related research, we explored the response of a chiral liquid to an orbital electric field, discovering that it yields results that diverge significantly from the Landau orbital limit. Our findings and analyses hold for Weyl semimetals in three-dimensional space, including those produced from three-dimensional topological insulators by applied magnetic fields, as well as recently identified Weyl semimetals like Mn$_3$Sn.

This research paper delves into the theoretical findings of devices that combine 
photonic crystals with optical cavities to enhance light emission from quantum 
dots by increasing the energy exchange between light and charge with the aid of 
polariton modes. Moreover, the mentioned setup allows for the reduction of directed 
emission into surrounding space by focusing on internal modes of nanowires and 
defining emission spectra. Finally, the study discusses how to widen the spectral 
range of polariton modes within silicon-based photonic crystals by employing 
nonlinear interactions.

Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is utilized across solid-state systems.  Nucleation of defects, scars and folds in curved crystals, as well as rearrangements of cells within biological tissue, all exhibit this phenomenon.  A crucial aspect of theoretical models for screening involves the presence of a well-defined reference state, to which screening elements react in order to release tension.  However, amorphous materials, lacking such a reference point, still demonstrate screening effects resulting from plastic events which have a considerable influence on the mechanical behavior of the material.  A recent research study proposed that in amorphous solids, mechanical strain can either exhibit weak or strong screening effects resulting from varying levels of plastic event density.  At lower levels of plastic event density, the screening effect can be compared to that of an electric double layer, with similar features such as linear energy scaling and a finite screening length.  However, at higher plastic event densities, the screening effect begins to display non-linear behavior and the screening length becomes dependent on the applied strain, ultimately tending towards an infinite length at full deformation.  Through numerical simulations as well as experiments with amorphous metals and biological tissues, the theoretical model was verified.  These findings can lead to a deeper understanding of mechanical behavior in complex materials and living tissues.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between decoration at the top and hollow sites. Furthermore, the system's induced magnetism is thoroughly examined.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our objective is to create a straightforward simulation of a supernova event, enabling straightforward input of basic parameters to produce realistic results, thus facilitating simulations. This simulation tool, based on a simplified 2D representation, includes a striped gas distribution to take into account the snail shell appearance of Sgr A East. Our simulation suggests that a massive, radiative shock wave forms at the snail trail, with a density ratio of 10 to 100 times higher than surrounding space. Furthermore, our results indicate that the radiation from the central source, assumed to have a luminosity of 10 to 100 times the luminosity of the central parsec cluster, is responsible for the brightest part of the snail shell. Our simulations reveal that a radiation-dominated part travels faster and has higher velocities than radiation-poor strips, consistent with observed strip velocities in Sgr A East. Our model indicates that X-ray emission originates from the snail trail, with X-ray spectral patterns influenced by irradiation of gas by the central radiation source. Our results show that aged snail shell strips glow with a softer X-ray spectrum and decreased X-ray intensity, with older strips displaying these characteristics. The study examines various oversampling methods for classification problems with class imbalance. A key issue discussed is how to effectively enhance the minority class samples, thereby improving the performance of the learning model. The discussion centers around the performance of several oversampling methods, including traditional approaches like copies and replicas, as well as more innovative techniques like generating new samples based on tangent hyperplane principle or Gaussian mixture model, and modifying the decision boundary to expand minority class samples within a learned shape. A key focus of the study is the SMOTE algorithm, which is compared with its variations, including two popular adaptations: SMOTE-TanH and SMOTE-GME. Furthermore, the study proposes a novel adaptation, referred to as K-Adaptive Deep Distribution-Free SMOTE (KADDFS), which is designed to accommodate complex and multidimensional data distributions learned by classifiers. KADDFS is developed to bridge the gap between data adaptation and learning by applying a deep learning-based clustering method to identify minority and majority clusters, thereby facilitating the generation of new minority class samples through the adaptation of a deep distribution learned by the classifier. A comprehensive analysis of the proposed method is also presented, along with demonstrations of its superiority over other oversampling algorithms using real-world datasets.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also reveals disparities in COVID reporting by U.S. state and demographic.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a method using Fast Multipole Method can efficiently reduce the computational load to O(N). In our experiments, we explored the interaction of equal-mass binaries experiencing gravitational waves and merging particles at various resolutions, comparing results with post-Newtonian theory. Furthermore, we investigated supernova remnants within the very large array's 2019 dataset, substituting SPH with the finite volume method for comparison. By substituting FMM-SPH with the finite volume method in astrophysical simulations powered by graphics processing units, we assessed any potential discrepancies and evaluated their impact on astrophysical astrophysics during core-collapse supernovae and neutron star mergers. Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of cross-sectional ratios in electron proton collisions, drawing on JLab polarization experiments measuring the ratio of Sachs form factors in such interactions. Calculations considering a scenario with fully polarized, in-line initial and final protons have been carried out to analyze polarization transfer and compare results to an experiment measuring double-spin asymmetry in another process. Research found a significant $Q^2$ dependence influence on polarization transfer to the proton, which may be exploited in new experiments to determine the $G_E/G_M$ ratio. This also led to proposing an alternative method for extracting the $G_E/G_M$ ratio from such interactions and exploring the compatibility of our results with current data on the $G_E/G_M$ ratio.

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning method we propose initially creates synthetic state data by generating state transitions through random actions, which are then processed using the same training technique as the original model. This is done without requiring knowledge of the environment dynamics or the target model's action values. The results show our method achieves comparable performance using similar training methods, often outperforming existing techniques. Furthermore, our method successfully enables data-efficient learning across diverse continuous control tasks in random environments, learning policies directly from high-dimensional visual inputs.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been carried out using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The research explored final states in which the vector boson decays into electrons and neutrinos or into electrons and other electrons and neutrinos, and each Higgs boson decays into pairs of $b$-quarks. It analyzed both resonant and non-resonant production modes. For the non-resonant case, upper limits ranging from 360 to 75 femtobarns at a 95% confidence level were found, comparing to the predicted Standard Model values of 13.6 and 3.6 femtobarns respectively. For the resonant case, the expected upper limits at 95% confidence were between 471 and 31 femtobarns depending on the assumed Higgs self-coupling. In both cases, the research set new records for the most stringent constraints yet on non-resonant $hh$ production.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation, offer superior sensitivity and a wide detection range compared to other optically pumped magnetometers and classical variometers. This technology, initially developed for high-sensitivity seismic measurements, can also be applied to magnetic field measurements by making a few key adjustments. Primarily, this involves choosing suitable laser frequencies to create a population imbalance, thereby enabling the resonance follow mode and enhancing the magnetometer's sensitivity to variations in the magnetic field. Furthermore, by incorporating a lock-point method that involves stabilizing a population difference at a specific, optimal level, system stability and sensitivity can be significantly improved. Notably, the lock-point method enables the precise tuning of population differences, thereby enabling the optimal detection of magnetic field changes. Last but not least, by coupling the optomechanical system, which includes a quartz glass plate, to one of the optical co-propagating beams, one can accurately measure changes in the glass plate's density, temperature, and refractive index, as well as detect mechanical strains on the glass caused by external forces such as pressure. This magnetometer offers superior sensitivity and a significantly broader detection range compared to conventional piezometers and thermometers. Its capabilities extend to the measurement of very low-frequency changes in pressure, accurate determination of precise refractive index measurements, and the detection of mechanical strains resulting from, for example, the pressure-induced structural deformation of the glass plate. For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers under this condition.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model with a $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ hidden sector gauge sector, where the hidden sector neutralino is much lighter than the rest, resulting in a decay length allowing the neutralino to evade cosmological constraints. Within the (M,G) plane of the SUGRA model defining the mass and coupling relationships, regions satisfying the conditions exist that can account for dark matter and the dark matter annihilation cross section fits observed galactic rotation curves. Furthermore, a variant of moduli-dominated cosmology is presented with implications for gravitational dark matter and the baryon asymmetry, where the gravitino acts as a cold dark matter candidate in this scenario.

The main contributors provide solid evidence to demonstrate the existence of different types of algorithms for finding the most minimal refinement of a given tree decomposition. We start by showcasing a simple EPTAS, followed by a more complex PTAS that allows for a customizable time complexity. We also address the challenge of incorporating cluster editing into the generalized metric tree decomposition framework, while tackling the difficulties associated with defining and achieving approximate cluster editing solutions within this framework. We successfully apply the proposed PTAS to gain a deeper understanding of the originally presented EPTAS. Additionally, we provide substantial insights by comparing and contrasting the newly introduced techniques with those related to other graph refinement methods.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages often shrouded in mystery.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-pattern gaseous detectors, time-resolution can be employed to track the track of a recoiling nucleus. We propose a new method, based on a detailed simulation, that extracts the direction of nuclear recoils from the temporal development of PMGD signals. This method can identify the direction with high precision (>10^5) for recoils produced by dark matter and from neutrino investigations, while revealing the detailed readout information. Our results also serve as a baseline for comparisons with experiments using similar detection methods or similar energy range.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the assessment process, our approach effectively considers the complexities of driving situations. Our proposed model employs Bayesian inference to combine expert opinions and derive a comprehensive understanding of driver behavior. Ultimately, our approach demonstrates the significance of incorporating expert knowledge in driver assessment, as evidenced by our case study's results.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two OCR models, leveraging either a single view (SV) or multiple views (MV) of text during model fine-tuning, alongside two novel evaluation metrics that have not been widely employed in contemporary OCR research.
A total of 56 team submissions participated in the competition, with the top three teams solving each problem respectively achieving validation and test F1 scores of 64.20% and 62.95%, and 55.96% and 53.71%.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about their temporal dynamics, prompting the development of novel methods in a recent study. By combining geometric and analytical techniques, a new understanding and classification of these fields has emerged, enabling the differentiation of their spatial and temporal configurations. Furthermore, a practical approach has been established for calculating probabilities associated with their highly complex trajectories.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$, and show that its algebraic component at critical point $m$ has bounded denominators as $\chi$ changes. This work refines a previous finding of Boecherer. Additionally, we investigate the holomorphy and convergence property of the interuniversal covering L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$.

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying barrier heights, which can be regulated with gate voltages, in addition to analyzing the effects of varying widths on the band gap and contact nature. The study uncovered periodic patterns in spin polarization in nanoribbons with wide band gaps, and observed that spin polarization is more prominent in shorter nanoribbons. The contrasting characteristics between spin and charge conductivities are more pronounced in nanoribbons with weak coupling between adjacent atoms, which results in a greater diversity of spin phenomena compared to graphene sheets.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number squared value should also be four times the smallest value of k^n-to-c, but he couldn't resolve the problem despite further research. He then posed another problem, stating that if you take the minimum value between two numbers, k to the fourth power and n to the four thirds, being less than one and n being greater than four, it should contain all cycles. Following the presentation of additional research, the problem was revised by stating that if you take the minimum value between two numbers, k to the fourth power and n to the four thirds, being less than one and n being greater than four, it should contain all cycles. 

Now researchers found a relationship between this problem, including graph symmetrical properties such as Hamiltonian and pancyclic characteristics, including pancyclic number and its relationship with the independence number. 

In terms of a number sequence called p-natural, including p-n, with p being a prime number and n being a whole number greater than or equal to two. Researchers found a relationship between this number sequence, including p-n, with p being a prime number and n being a whole number greater than or equal to two.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold collisions at a specific energy level (200 GeV) has been studied to understand the influence of the quadrupole structure that forms in heavy-ion collisions. Researchers found that the energy pattern of particles formed in these collisions is more complex than initially thought, exhibiting a directed flow pattern similar to that of a specific type of flow. A theoretical model that takes into account the interaction between two particles has been used to explain the observed pattern, suggesting that the particles are affected by the structure that forms in the collision, thereby changing their initial trajectory. In contrast, similar studies at a different energy level found that the energy pattern of particles formed in deuterium-tungsten collisions is comparable to that of a single particle, indicating that the particles are minimally affected by the interaction. A change in the structure that forms in the collision was observed, showing that the particles are more likely to move in a specific direction when the initial particles are oriented in a particular way.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as the groundwork for numerous applications across diverse scientific and engineering fields. Despite its high accuracy, ASK has a computational disadvantage when dealing with multi-dimensional systems due to its complexity in matrix operations. To mitigate this limitation, we modified the time integration process of ASK to utilize sparse grid approaches and developed a new algorithm, referred to as the adaptive sparse-grid Koopman method (ASKG). Throughout several tests, ASKG consistently outperformed traditional time integration methods in terms of computational efficiency while maintaining a high level of precision. Notably, ASKG approximates the solution of multi-dimensional systems using a lower-order polynomial than its single-dimensional counterpart, thus significantly enhancing its computational efficiency. To validate the effectiveness of ASKG, we applied the method to various complex dynamical systems, including those featuring chaotic dynamics, soft-sensor applications, and uncertain parameters. Ultimately, we assessed the uncertainty bounds associated with the ASKG-based estimates using the Kotani-type inequality.

This review is focused on providing an introduction to resonance parameters in one-photon processes, reviewing their theoretical and experimental history, and highlighting advancements, applications, and ongoing challenges. A comprehensive discussion of one-photon transition processes, mathematical methods used to extract resonance parameters, and contemporary applications will be presented. Furthermore, modern theoretical and experimental aspects related to extracting resonance parameters via one-photon transitions will be examined.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference coupling have the same support. Considering that structured stochastic processes often result in degenerate scenarios where the solution may encompass an entire space, a different approach is employed. By developing a dual algorithm, this work provides a primer on how to demonstrate the algorithm's convergence in almost all instances, whereas previous studies focused primarily on the Cotar-Lassas-Laptev-Schulze approach. Although the new algorithm was inspired by the Cotar-LassavrySchulzevagantz proof, important differences do exist. Ultimately, determining whether the Schrödinger problem has a solution or not is a complex, outstanding issue that remains to be resolved.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states with contributions excluded due to calorimeter data, and a jet filtering technique is applied to reduce background influences. The calculated t¯t cross-section is found to be 67.5 pb with an uncertainty of 5.3 pb, aligning with theoretical predictions from the Standard Model of 66.8 ± 2.2 pb.

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system or environment would need to be well-defined before measuring a central entity's properties. 
However, our research presents an alternative view where the central entity itself causes instability in the surrounding system due to their energetic alignment, leading to a regular pattern of energy release among the surrounding entities. 
Through theoretical analysis, we found that this instability causes variations in the central entity's energy patterns, allowing for the emergence of distinct statistical patterns, such as non-Gaussian distributions, heat resistance, and long-tailed frequency patterns, beyond basic thermal behavior predictions. 
Notably, these effects can be observed in systems where the central entity interacts with a disordered bath and is within it, and in the central entity itself, depending on the central entity's resilience. 
To validate these findings, we created and analyzed numerous simulated systems, resulting in a new classification of central entities and surrounding environments and their possible interactions.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ are specified that guarantee 
${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ meets the requirement ${u}_{p,b,c}(z) \prec (1+Az)/(1+Bz)$. This yields conditions 
for $(-4\kappa/c)({u}_{p,b,c}(z)-1)$, $c \neq 0$, to be close-to-convex and for ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ 
to be Janowski convex as well as $z{u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ to be Janowski starlike in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity and dynamic social environment, which fosters innovation and productivity. Although face-to-face interactions have been hindered by the COVID-19 pandemic, it's essential to understand the long-term effects on urban attractiveness and attractivity. This research combines data analysis and computational modeling, incorporating employment data, flight records, and COVID-19 infection rates, to study the relationship between a city's economic appeal and social meetups. A 3D framework is proposed to explore factors like encounter probability, geographical distance, and social connections that influence a city's attractivity score. To calculate encounter probabilities, the city of Barcelona is used as a case study, which allows for calibration of a multi-agent simulation model to predict each city's attractivity score. Furthermore, proposed models provide accurate predictions not only for cities in Spain but also for a broader set of 128 cities. Therefore, the attractivity score model can be a valuable tool for decision-makers to assess a city's economic and social potential.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split Multiplicative Schwarz Newton, operates in a sequential two-step process:
initially, an approximate update of pressure and saturation is achieved through
a preconditioning step by resolving sub-problems in succession; secondly, a
global Newton update is applied using coupled conservation equations and flow
rules. Due to its inner iterative process, the FSMP preconditioning approach is
capable of providing an optimal convergence acceleration in large-scale two-phase
flow modeling and transport simulations. Various case studies have been conducted
using real-world field data to illustrate the efficiency of this novel algorithm.
Subsequent studies examined its application within model frameworks that lack
optimality but feature computationally manageable models such as the ST stokes-klinkenberg model. Results obtained reveal that the FSMP preconditioning
approach significantly accelerates convergence in models both with and without
optimality in the model framework. Additionally, numerical findings suggest that
the FSMP preconditioning approach is well-suited for diverse two-phase flow and
transport applications within porous media.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life forms to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specific polarization properties that allow for the identification and separation of enantiomers within molecular pairs. Developing an optical cavity capable of efficiently interacting with chiral matter is therefore crucial, and is achieved through the creation of an atomically thin, chiral monolayer made of boron nitride and embedded in a hybrid photonic circuit. When chiral light is applied to this entity, it induces a photonic effect known as the Kerr response, allowing for the separation of enantiomers within molecular pairs. This innovation holds the potential to revolutionize future optical circuits by integrating chirality-based functions and could have significant implications for various applications in life science research at the molecular level.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model. This match, significantly influenced by boundary terms, extends to annulus amplitudes. We also derive the boundary Schwarzian theory from the Liouville CFT and further establish an equivalence between the two-dimensional string theory and a specific time-dependent matrix model. This relation is then generalized to the case of two-dimensional de-Sitter JT gravity.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This research extends our previous solutions by applying the Einstein equations to the warp drive metric, incorporating both a perfect fluid source and a perfect fluid source with a cosmological constant, including a special case with a vanishing cosmological constant, which has a finite density perfect fluid source. However, any physically meaningful solution we found had a vacuum-filled region that violates the speed limit, whereas the Einstein equations require a smooth and continuous spacetime. Furthermore, we observed that requiring a matter-filled spacetime, as opposed to a vacuum-filled spacetime, does not suffice to eliminate the warp bubble's speed-limit-violating region.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited understanding of their infrastructure's current state. Most cities lack accurate digital data on their underground systems (electricity, water, natural gas), hindering construction project planning. To overcome these issues, a new framework called GUIDES has been introduced to manage and process data for underground infrastructure systems. This enables a wide range of users, from administrators to workers, to make data-driven decisions. GUIDES consists of several key components, including specialized apps for collecting and processing different types of data as well as a core platform, all integrated into an unified system. This framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through its current implementation in Toronto's underground infrastructure system.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized the interaction between optical dipoles and the ions' spin, enabling the characterization of their transverse movement. This was done by comparing the experimentally measured effects on spin dephasing with theoretical predictions, resulting in accurate estimations of temperature levels consistent with previously documented standards, including both laser cooling constraints and earlier research methods. Additionally, our approach enabled the differentiation between the ions' initial motion states as either thermal or coherent, providing crucial insight. This analysis technique was also utilized to measure, for the first time, the environmental influence on the ions' movement in a specific type of Penning trap. This was accomplished by comparing, for the first time, the experimental outcomes with theoretical predictions at low thermal levels, resulting in an estimated environmental decoherence rate.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS signals is computationally difficult. Our innovative method combines specific scattering factors with detailed calculations of the electrostatic field caused by the tip. Our results show that the electrostatic sampling plays a significant role in measuring Raman signal strength. By demonstrating for Au(111) that the entire Raman spectrum can be explained through electrostatic sampling, along with C-H bond characterization, it's concluded that the intensity of TERS is primarily determined by two factors: the intensity of the primary laser and the shape of the electrostatic field caused by the tip. Our research also enables the simulation of the C-H bond Raman signal of Au(111) that lacks a sp$^{2}$ hybridized carbon atom by simply adding the contribution of the primary laser. Additionally, our research contributes to resolving controversies surrounding TERS experiments by providing precise calculations of the C-H signal of Au(111). Our research also sheds light on various factors such as the shape of the primary laser, the shape of the electrostatic field caused by the tip, and the movement of the target molecule during scanning, which can affect the accuracy of the TERS signal.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, with particular attention to how their emission relates to M 31. Through radio-continuum data and global photometry at 18.6 and 24.6 GHz, we sought to find and quantify the AME contribution, taking into account the impact of thermal radiation from dust. Failing to detect significant AME signals in three out of four galaxies (with upper limits set at 50 Jy rms), we were only able to determine a weak, tentative AME contribution for NGC 3627. Our observations suggest that the rotation measure in the central regions of our target galaxies is close to zero or unmeasurable. With an upper limit of 5.7 mK rm, our research sets a new constraint for the spin temperature of AME grains, specifically at a wavelength of 30.9 mm. Our findings conflict with prior studies suggesting that AME is more prevalent in spiral galaxies with stronger magnetic fields.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and additional neutron scattering experiments. In contrast to the previously assumed, albeit widely adopted model of entropy involving disorder across the high-symmetry phase's mirror plane, it is now clear that this simplistic model is invalid. Instead, it is discovered that the significant entropy originates from the low-frequency wobbling of ammonium ions in their oxygen sites, which results in a large degeneracy of phonon density of states. This finding serves as a prime representation of how quantum fluctuations can often be crucial in understanding crystal dynamics. Furthermore, the observed phonon behavior serves as a benchmark for assessing the performance of density functional methods in predicting quantum systems.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching when the available options aren't clearly defined or aren't preferred over other options.  A recent paper suggests that a well-designed probabilistic learning model, incorporating a specific type of uncertainty and a strategic approach, can effectively explain a range of learning behaviors, including probability-matching, in various tasks of different levels of complexity.  A study compared the performance of this new model to that of other established models and found that it surpassed them in explaining a wide range of data, while also showcasing its ability to naturally produce variability and adaptability in responses.  Further analysis revealed that the new model can effectively simulate more intricate mental processes, like decision-making in situations of high or low uncertainty, and that these processes correlate with variations in performance.  Overall, the study highlights the potential of incorporating probabilistic characteristics and strategic approaches in learning theories to better comprehend complex learning behaviors.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the Witting configuration's attributes.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing a comprehensive analysis for one-dimensional curves. By improving existing results, the research offers multiple tradeoffs between approximation quality, preprocessing efficiency, and query speed. Key outcomes include achieving the same performance as the previously best result for an improved approximation factor while also reaching the previously best result with reduced query complexity. Additionally, lower bounds on the data structure's efficiency were derived using the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current techniques combine noisy data from multiple runs to produce an estimated noise model. Nevertheless, the success of these methods often relies on the assumption that all runs have the same noise model, which may not be the case, particularly when running large-scale experiments that take advantage of parallel processing. This limitation is addressed by a new method, known as adaptive ABC, which leverages the capabilities of artificial brain circuits to mitigate errors in near-term devices. By utilizing a wide distribution of qubit mappings, the method reduces the likelihood of misestimating noise patterns. Despite its name suggesting global noise models, the adaptive approach allows for the estimation of local noise patterns through the use of bootstrapping, which is illustrated by experiments involving real-world quantum processors.

When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on assistive teleoperation and shared control focuses on developing methods for the robot to determine the desired task based on human joystick inputs.
